 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Environmental information  > ESRS E1 Climate changeSeveral of the targets in the transition plan are based 
on emissions intensity, and in line with the phasing-in 
period for reporting on the value chain for the financial 
sector (ESRS E1 10.2, 132 and 133), which applies to 
the first three reporting years under the CSRD, DNB is 
not reporting absolute figures for 2030. This is in line 
with the practice of most financial institutions, as in the 
sector it makes the most sense to report the greenhouse 
gas emissions reduction target in the form of intensities. 
DNB has therefore prioritised obtaining and collating 
data based on emissions intensity, instead of absolute 
values. DNB has further not calculated the proportion of 
Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions for each sector in the loan 
and investment portfolio, or the sectors’ total quantitative 
contributions to achieve the targets for reduction of 
greenhouse gas emissions. This is because the transition 
plan does not have a concrete pathway for each sector in 
order to achieve net-zero emissions. The methodology, 
choice of pathway and assumptions for the targets are 
described under Transition plan (ESRS E1-1). 
The targets in the transition plan have been validated by 
DNV. The purpose of the validation has been to achieve an 
external assessment that confirms that the 2030 targets 
in the transition plan are science-based and prepared 
in line with the methods and climate scenarios used. An 
assessment was further made during the validation process 
as to how the targets are consistent with the work of 
limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees. Based on its review, 
DNV has concluded that most of DNB’s 2030 targets are 
consistent with assessment criteria associated with the 
Paris Agreement and the 1.5-degree target, including 
the choice of climate scenarios, baseline years and the 
methodology for estimating emissions. For information 
about the scenario analyses that have been used and how 
the targets are consistent with the work to limit global 
warming to 1.5 degrees, see Transition plan (ESRS E1-1)

title: Description of developments during the year for each target
heading: 3.11.2 Description of developments during the year for each target
start_phrase: In 2024, the emissions intensity was 3.03 kg CO2e/m²/year for the entire home mortgage portfolio, which is somewhat down from the baseline year 2019 (3.69 kg CO2e/m²/year), and down from 2023 (3.75 kg CO2e/m²/year).
summary:
- Reporting approach and methodology
  - Transition plan targets are intensity-based; absolute 2030 figures are not reported due to ESRS E1 value-chain reporting phase-in under CSRD.
  - DNB prioritised emissions-intensity data over absolute values and has not broken down Scope 1, 2, 3 shares per sector or quantified sectoral contributions to portfolio targets, as no sector-specific net-zero pathways are set yet.
  - Methods, pathways, and assumptions are referenced under Transition plan (ESRS E1-1).

- External validation
  - DNV validated the 2030 targets, concluding most are science-based and consistent with the Paris Agreement/1.5°C, including scenario choices, baseline years, and emissions estimation methodology.

- Portfolio progress and key 2024/2023 metrics (intensity unless noted; ESRS 2 BP-2; PCAF data quality in parentheses)
  - Mortgages: 3.03 kg CO2e/m²/year in 2024 (vs 3.69 in 2019; 3.75 in 2023); 100% estimates; PCAF 3.2.
  - Housing cooperatives: 2.78 kg CO2e/m²/year in 2024 (vs 3.65 in 2019); 100% estimates; PCAF 3.6.
  - Commercial real estate: 2.97 kg CO2e/m²/year in 2024 (vs 3.68 in 2019); 100% estimates; PCAF 3.9.
  - Shipping: 2023 loan-weighted AER up 3.2%; 100% actual; PCAF 1.0. Increase driven by high LNG activity amid tight energy markets; most other vessel types improved.
  - Motor vehicles: 56 g CO2e/km in 2024 (37.1% below 2019); 100% estimates; PCAF 3.9.
  - Steel: 0.87 t CO2e/t steel in 2023, higher than 2019 baseline 0.22; 100% actual; PCAF 1.0.
  - Oil and gas: committed lending down 21% vs 2019; exposure remains dynamic due to market factors.
  - Power generation: 2019 baseline 29.3 kg CO2e/MWh; no reduction target set due to low baseline. 2024 intensity 14.1 kg CO2e/MWh; 27% estimates/73% actual; PCAF 2.8.
  - Salmon farming: Scope 1–3 intensity rose from 4.59 kg CO2e/kg HOG (2019) to 9.96 (2023); 100% actual; PCAF 1.7.
  - DNB Asset Management (listed equity and corporate bonds): share of portfolio companies with SBTs increased from 30% (2023) to 36.5% (2024); 70 engagement dialogues with top 25 emitters to drive SBT adoption toward the 2030 target (58% AUM with SBTs).
  - DNB Livsforsikring (listed equity and corporate bonds, WACI): carbon intensity at end-2024 reflects a 46% reduction since 2019 and a 3% decrease vs 2023; drivers include portfolio allocation and sector mix changes; 96% actual/4% estimates. SBT coverage rose to 23% in 2024 (behind the 53% by 2030 target but improving faster than the MSCI World).
  - DNB Næringseiendom: 4.11 kg CO2e/m² in 2024 (vs 7.2 in 2019); reductions from operations, projects, and asset sales; Scope 2 is 98% actual; no Scope 1 estimation.

- Sustainable finance mobilisation
  - Target to mobilise NOK 1,500 billion by 2030 through lending and facilitation for the sustainable transition; products and inclusion criteria are defined within the transition plan framework.
text:
Description of developments during the year 
for each target:
Mortgages
In 2024, the emissions intensity was 3.03 kg CO2e/m²/year 
for the entire home mortgage portfolio, which is 
somewhat down from the baseline year 2019 (3.69 kg 
CO2e/m²/year), and down from 2023 (3.75 kg CO2e/
m²/year). Of these values, 100 per cent are estimates 
(ESRS 2 BP-2). The PCAF score was 3.2. 
Housing cooperatives
The portfolio’s emissions intensity declined to 
2.78 kg CO2e/m2/year in 2024 from 3.65 in 2019. Of 
these values, 100 per cent are estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2). 
The PCAF score was 3.6. Commercial real estate
The portfolio’s calculated emissions intensity for 2024 
was 2.97 kg CO2e/m2/year, which is lower than the 
emissions intensity in 2019 of 3.68 kg CO2e/m2/year. Of 
these values, 100 per cent are estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2). 
The PCAF score was 3.9. 
Shipping
After a substantial reduction in 2022, in 2023 DNB noted 
an increase of 3.2 per cent in loan-weighted AER. Of 
these values, 100 per cent are actual data (ESRS 2 BP-2). 
The PCAF score was 1.0. 
The main reason for the increase is circumstances in the 
market in certain segments (for certain vessel types), 
including very high activity in the LNG segment (transport 
of liquid natural gas) in a pressured energy market in 
2023. Most of the other vessels in the portfolio show 
continued reductions in emissions intensity. 
Motor vehicles
In 2024, the portfolio’s emissions intensity was 
56 g CO2e/km, which is a 37.1 per cent reduction 
compared with the baseline year 2019. Of these values, 
100 per cent are estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2). The PCAF 
score was 3.9. 
Steel
The emissions intensity of DNB’s steel portfolio was 
0.87 tonnes CO2e/tonne steel in 2023. in 2019. This is 
slightly higher than the 2019 baseline of 0.22 tonnes 
CO2e/tonne steel. Of these values, 100 per cent are 
actual data (ESRS 2 BP-2). The PCAF score was 1.0. 
Oil and gas
At the end of 2024, DNB’s committed lending amounts 
had declined by 21 per cent, compared with 2019. 
It is important to point out that DNB’s committed lending 
exposure is dynamic and subject to fluctuations, among 
other things, due to macro conditions and event-driven 
situations that are typical for the oil and gas industry.
Power generation
The baseline value of DNB’s power generation portfolio 
for 2019 was 29.3 kg CO2e/MWh, and given the low 
baseline value, DNB has not set an emissions reduction 
target, as it would limit the flexibility it needs to support 
customers with credible transition strategies. The 
portfolio’s emissions intensity was reduced further to 
14.1 kg CO2e/MWh by year-end 2024. Of these values, 
27 per cent are estimates and 73 per cent are actual data 
(ESRS 2 BP-2). The PCAF score was 2.8. 
119
DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Environmental information  > ESRS E1 Climate changeSalmon farming
The portfolio’s average emissions intensity for Scope 1, 2 
and 3 emissions went from 4.59 kg CO2e/kg HOG (Head-
On-Gutted) in 2019 to 9.96 in 2023. Of these values, 
100 per cent are actual data (ESRS 2 BP-2). The PCAF 
score was 1.7. 
DNB Asset Management: listed shares and 
corporate bonds
By the end of 2023, 30 per cent of companies in 
the portfolio had SBTs, and at the end of 2024, the 
proportion had increased to 36.5 per cent. This means 
that the company is well on the way to achieving the 
target that 58 per cent of the company’s AUM must have 
SBTs for emissions reductions by 2030.
In 2024, DAM conducted 70 dialogues to influence the 
25 companies in the portfolio that contribute the most 
to emissions in DAM. This is to contribute to companies 
setting realistic and science-based targets, which in 
turn contributes to DAM achieving the targets set in the 
transition plan. 
DNB Livsforsikring: listed shares and corporate 
bonds – weighted average carbon intensity 
(WACI)
At the end of 2024, DNB Livsforsikring measured a 
carbon intensity of 58.1 per cent. This is a decrease of 
3 per cent from the end of 2023. Since the beginning 
of the measurements in 2019, DNB Livsforsikring has 
reduced emissions by 46 per cent, which means that 
the company is well on track to achieving the target of 
a 55 per cent reduction by 2030. The marginal decline 
in 2024 is mainly due to allocations in the portfolio and 
a changed sectoral mix in the market index and the 
portfolio of DNB Livsforsikring. Carbon-intensive sectors 
like energy and raw materials performed weakly in 2024, 
compared with sectors with relatively low emissions, 
like communication, consumption and technology. As 
a result, carbon-intensive companies made up a lower 
proportion of DNB Livsforsikring’s portfolio by the end of 
2024, which contributed to a reduction in the emissions 
intensity. Of these values, 4 per cent are estimates and 
96 per cent are actual data (ESRS 2 BP-2). 
DNB Livsforsikring: listed shares and corporate 
bonds, proportion of AUM with SBTs 
At the end of 2024, 23 per cent of the companies in DNB 
Livsforsikring’s portfolio had SBTs. This is a considerable 
increase from 2022 and 2023, where the proportion of 
companies was 15 and 18 per cent, respectively. DNB Livsforsikring is slightly behind schedule in terms of 
the target of 53 per cent of the company’s AUM having 
SBTs by 2030. However, the increase is still larger than in 
the market overall, measured by the MSCI World Index. 
DNB Næringseiendom
In 2024, the portfolio’s carbon intensity was 
4.11 kg CO2e/m2, down from 7.2 kg CO2e/m2 in 2019. 
The reductions come from the ordinary operation of 
buildings, execution of projects and sales of buildings. 
98 per cent of the values in Scope 2 came from actual 
data. There was no estimation of Scope 1 values (ESRS 2 
BP-2).

title: Mobilise NOK 1 500 billion to the sustainable transition, through lending and facilitation, by 2030
heading: 3.11.3 Mobilise NOK 1 500 billion to the sustainable transition, through lending and facilitation, by 2030
start_phrase: The target to mobilise NOK 1 500 billion to the sustainable transition, through lending and facilitation, is included in DNB’s transition plan.
summary:
- Context: Excerpt from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report (Sustainability report, ESRS E1 Climate change) covering portfolio emissions, target progress, sustainable finance mobilization, sustainable products, and GHG accounting.
- Salmon farming portfolio: Average Scope 1–3 emissions intensity rose from 4.59 to 9.96 kg CO2e/kg HOG (2019–2023); 100% actual data (ESRS 2 BP-2); PCAF score 1.7.
- DNB Asset Management (listed shares and corporate bonds): Companies with science-based targets (SBTs) increased from 30% (end-2023) to 36.5% (end-2024), progressing toward 58% AUM with SBTs by 2030. Conducted 70 engagement dialogues in 2024 with top 25 emitters to drive realistic SBTs aligned with DAM’s transition plan.
- DNB Livsforsikring (listed shares and corporate bonds, WACI): Carbon intensity at 58.1 at end-2024, down 3% from 2023 and 46% since 2019, on track for 55% reduction by 2030. Decline driven by allocations and sector mix shifts favoring lower-emission sectors. Data quality: 96% actual, 4% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- DNB Livsforsikring SBT coverage: 23% of portfolio companies had SBTs at end-2024 (up from 15% in 2022 and 18% in 2023); slightly behind the 53% AUM-by-2030 target but improving faster than the MSCI World.
- DNB Næringseiendom: Portfolio carbon intensity reduced to 4.11 kg CO2e/m2 in 2024 from 7.2 in 2019, driven by operations, projects, and asset sales; Scope 2 data 98% actual, no estimation for Scope 1 (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- Sustainable finance mobilization: Target to mobilize NOK 1,500 billion by 2030 via lending and facilitation. Detailed inclusion criteria across:
  - Bonds (green/social/sustainability; sustainability-linked; unlabeled renewables),
  - Advisory (debt; equity and M&A for renewables-related),
  - Loans (green loans; sustainability-linked loans; unlabeled renewables),
  - Guarantees (green),
  - Environmentally friendly transport (zero-emission vehicles; excludes fossil-fuel transport).
  In 2024, NOK 190 billion mobilized; cumulative NOK 751.8 billion since 2020. Growth led by green loans (real estate, renewables), plus increases in SLLs, EV financing, and sustainable bonds.
- Mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile (DAM): Strategic aim for NOK 200 billion AUM by 2025 and 50% of net flows to such products. Approaches include climate criteria, exclusions, broader E/S focus, SDG alignment; includes SFDR Articles 8 and 9. 2024 saw new launches and reclassifications, supporting AUM growth to NOK 137.8 billion (from NOK 124.3 billion in 2023). ESRS 2 BP-2 note: From Q3 2024, target expanded to include discretionary mandates (SFDR 8/9); no restatement; three Luxembourg Article 8 low-carbon funds added in Q4.
- Greenhouse gas accounting (ESRS E1-6): For financial institutions, primary emissions are financed emissions (Scope 3, category 15). DNB reports Scope 3 only for category 15; other Scope 3 categories omitted. 2024 established as the baseline year for financed emissions (pending future scope consistency). Scope 1 and 2 cover DNB’s own operations. Baseline years for some climate targets remain 2019 and 2022.
text:
The target to mobilise NOK 1 500 billion to the 
sustainable transition, through lending and facilitation, 
is included in DNB’s transition plan. DNB is able to be 
a driving force in and support this transition through 
financing, advisory services and investment in products 
and services linked to the sustainable transition. The table 
below provides an overview of the products that are 
included in the financing target and associated inclusion 
criteria.

title: Mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile - Introduction
heading: 3.11.4 Mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile
start_phrase: In DAM, mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile make an important contribution to achieving the ambition of increasing the total AUM in mutual funds and portfolios of this kind to NOK 200 billion in 2025.
summary: Overview of DAM’s sustainability-profile mutual funds and portfolios, including 2025 targets to grow AUM to NOK 200 billion and achieve 50% of net flows into these products; scope covers strategies with explicit sustainability considerations such as climate-focused criteria, exclusion of high carbon emitters, broader climate/environment themes, and investments aligned with UN SDGs. Included vehicles are SFDR Article 9 portfolios and Article 8 funds with a required share of sustainable investments or promotion of environmental/social characteristics via extended exclusions. In 2024, DAM launched new sustainability-profile funds and reclassified existing ones (using SFDR methodology without statutory auditor assurance), driving AUM growth; returns were good, and institutional clients increased purchases of fixed-income funds. Holdings increased to NOK 137.8 billion from NOK 124.3 billion.
text:
Mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability 
profile 
In DAM, mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability 
profile make an important contribution to achieving the 
ambition of increasing the total AUM in mutual funds 
and portfolios of this kind to NOK 200 billion in 2025. In 
addition, the aim is for 50 per cent of net flows of AUM to 
go to mutual funds with a sustainability profile in 2025. 
The targets for AUM in mutual funds and portfolios with 
a sustainability profile cover mutual funds and portfolios 
that include specific sustainability considerations in their 
investment strategy. The mutual funds can focus on climate 
criteria, exclude companies with high greenhouse carbon 
emissions, or take a broader perspective that covers both 
climate and environmental aspects. The overall objective 
is to invest in companies that are well positioned for the 
green shift, either through own operations or through 
the products and services they offer. In addition, some 
mutual funds focus on environmental and social targets 
through investment in companies that are in line with 
one or more of the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs). The portfolios that have been included are those 
that have been managed in line with the requirements in 
Article 9 of the SFDR, in addition to Article 8 funds, which 
have a required proportion of sustainable investments or 
that promote environmental and/or social characteristics 
through extended exclusion criteria, for example, the 
exclusion of companies with high carbon emissions. 
In 2024, DAM launched several new mutual funds with a 
sustainability profile, in addition to reclassifying existing 
funds because, for example, their exclusion criteria had 
been extended 14. This has contributed to positive growth 
in AUM. The return on mutual funds with a sustainability 
14 The mutual funds have been reclassified using SFDR methodology, without being assured by a statutory auditor.profile has been good during the year. Among the 
institutional customers, however, DAM observed an 
increase in sales of fixed-income funds. The holdings at 
the end of 2023 were NOK 137.8 billion, compared with 
NOK 124.3 billion at year-end 2023.

title: ESRS 2 BP-2 Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances: Changes in the scope of mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile
heading: 3.11.4.1 ESRS 2 BP-2 Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances: Changes in the scope of mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile
start_phrase: From the third quarter of 2024, the target of increasing the AUM in mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile was changed to NOK 200 billion.
summary:
- DNB mobilised NOK 190 billion in sustainable finance in 2024 through lending and facilitation, bringing the cumulative total since 2020 to NOK 751.8 billion toward a 2030 target of NOK 1,500 billion.
- Year-on-year growth was NOK 19 billion, with the strongest percentage increases in green loans for green real estate and renewable energy; sustainability-linked loans, environmentally friendly transport, and sustainable bonds also grew.
- DNB Asset Management (DAM) is pursuing an ambition to reach NOK 200 billion in AUM for mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile by 2025 and target 50% of net flows into such products. These strategies include SFDR Article 8 and 9 approaches, climate-focused criteria, exclusions (e.g., high carbon emitters), broader E/S characteristics, and SDG-aligned investments.
- In 2024, DAM launched new sustainability-profiled funds and reclassified existing ones (based on SFDR methodology, not auditor-assured), contributing to AUM growth; holdings rose to NOK 137.8 billion from NOK 124.3 billion the prior year, amid increased institutional interest in fixed-income funds.
- ESRS 2 BP-2: From Q3 2024, the NOK 200 billion AUM target was expanded to include discretionary mandates under SFDR Articles 8 and 9; no historical restatement. Three new Luxembourg funds on a low-carbon platform (SFDR Article 8, excluding high-emission companies) were added in Q4.
- ESRS E1-6: For greenhouse gas accounting, DNB identifies financed emissions (Scope 3, category 15 – Investments) as the primary source of emissions and omits other Scope 3 categories. 2024 serves as the baseline year for financed emissions reporting; comparisons will begin from 2025, while other climate targets retain 2019 and 2022 baselines. Scope 1 and 2 cover DNB’s own operations.
text:
ESRS 2 BP-2 Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances: 
Changes in the scope of mutual funds and portfolios with a 
sustainability profile
From the third quarter of 2024, the target of increasing 
the AUM in mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability 
profile was changed to NOK 200 billion. The target was 
expanded and now also covers discretionary mandates, 
as defined in Articles 8 and 9 of the SFDR. No history 
has been restated, as the inclusion applies from the third 
quarter. Three new mutual funds registered in Luxembourg 
have been included from the fourth quarter. These three 
are on DAM’s low-carbon platform. This means that the 
mutual funds do not invest in companies with high carbon 
emissions, and they are regulated by Article 8 of the SFDR.

title: Greenhouse gas accounting - Introduction
heading: 3.12 Greenhouse gas accounting
start_phrase: For a financial institution, the downstream value chain is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions, as emissions are generated through financial services, investments and lending.
summary: Introduces DNB’s ESRS E1-6 greenhouse gas accounting, stating that for financial institutions the downstream value chain is the largest source of emissions via financed emissions; accordingly, DNB reports Scope 3 only for GHG Protocol category 15 (Investments) and omits other Scope 3 categories. It identifies negative impacts, risks and opportunities tied to financed emissions, sets 2024 as the baseline year (no prior category 15 reporting) for comparisons from 2025, and notes that targets under ESRS E1-4 use 2019 and 2022 baselines. Reported 2024 metrics are: Scope 1 gross 67 t CO2e; Scope 2 gross 1,379 t CO2e (location-based) and 384 t CO2e (market-based); Scope 3 gross 25,515,575 t CO2e entirely from category 15 Investments, including 1,637 t CO2e from DNB Næringseiendom self-owned investment property (location-based). Total emissions are 25,517,021 t CO2e (location-based) and 25,516,026 t CO2e (market-based). Scope 1 and 2 cover DNB’s own operations.
text:
Greenhouse gas accounting
ESRS E1-6 Gross Scope 1, 2, 3 and total greenhouse gas 
emissions
For a financial institution, the downstream value chain is the 
largest source of greenhouse gas emissions, as emissions 
are generated through financial services, investments and 
lending. DNB’s negative impacts, risks and opportunities 
associated with greenhouse gas emissions have also 
been identified in DNB’s downstream value chain, through 
financed emissions. Financed emissions fall under Scope 3, 
category 15 Investments, in the Greenhouse Gas Protocol 
(GHG Protocol), and this is the category the Group reports 
on for Scope 3 emissions in the greenhouse gas accounting. 
The remaining Scope 3 categories have therefore been 
omitted from DNB’s greenhouse gas accounting. 
DNB has not previously reported emissions in category 
15, and therefore does not have a baseline year to 
compare with. From 2025, DNB will be able to compare 
developments in greenhouse gas emissions with the 
reporting in 2024, as long as there are no major changes 
to what is included. The figure for 2024 has therefore 
been set as the baseline. Note that the baseline years for 
the targets that have been reported in the texts relating 
to targets associated with mitigation of and adaptation to 
climate change (ESRS E1-4) are 2019 and 2022. 
The figures for Scope 1 and 2 emissions apply to DNB’s 
own operations.

title: Scope 1
heading: 3.12.1.1 Scope 1
start_phrase: DNB’s Scope 1 emissions include use of fuel from rental cars used by DNB’s employees.
summary:
- Scope and standards: Reports Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, SF6, HFCs, PFCs) converted to CO2e, calculated under the GHG Protocol using an operational control (control) approach.
- Scope 1 boundary and results: Includes fuel use from rental/leased cars used by employees; 2024 emissions total 67 tCO2e.
- Scope 1 methodology: Based on total mileage in leasing agreements, converted to litres and kWh; calculations by a third party. Emission factors: petrol and diesel tailored to Nordic/Luxembourg contexts; hybrids use combined fuel and electricity factors. Sources include DEFRA 2024, Norwegian Environment Agency, and IEA 2024. Electricity use from hybrids/EVs is accounted for in Scope 2.
- Scope 2 boundary: Indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heating, and cooling; reported using both location-based and market-based methods.
- Scope 2 location-based results and methods: 2024 total 1,379 tCO2e, of which electricity accounts for 1,247 tCO2e. Primarily uses metered activity data; estimates applied for smaller Norwegian sites (based on other offices’ consumption) and international representative offices (based on Odyssee-Mure per-employee statistics). Emission factors are country/region-specific IEA 2024 values.
- Context: Extract from DNB Group Annual Report 2024, Sustainability Report, ESRS E1 Climate change.
text:
Scope 1 
DNB’s Scope 1 emissions include use of fuel from 
rental cars used by DNB’s employees. The total Scope 1 
emissions in 2024 were 67 t CO2e. 
The calculation is based on the total mileage in leasing 
agreements and the average fuel and electricity 
consumption per kilometre. The mileage data from 
the leasing agreements is then converted into litres 
and kWh. The calculations are performed by a third 
party. The emissions factor used for petrol represents a 
common form of petrol in the Nordics and Luxembourg. 
The emissions factor used for diesel reflects the Nordic 
market better than a general diesel factor. For hybrid 
vehicles, a combination of the emissions factors for fuel 
and electricity have been used. The fuel factors have 
been obtained from the Department for Environment, 
Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA, 2024) and the Norwegian 
Environment Agency, and the electricity factor is from the 
IEA in 2024. Note that the electricity consumption from 
hybrid vehicles and electric vehicles is reported under 
Scope 2.

Scope 2

relating to purchased energy, heating and cooling. The

Scope 2
DNB’s Scope 2 emissions include indirect emissions 
relating to purchased energy, heating and cooling. The

title: Location-based method
heading: 3.12.1.2.1 Location-based method
start_phrase: When using the location-based method, DNB’s total Scope 2 emissions were 1 379 t CO2e in 2024.
summary:
- Focus: Reporting limits and calculation methods for DNB Group’s greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting under ESRS E1.
- Gases covered: CO2, CH4, N2O, SF6, HFCs, and PFCs, all converted to CO2e across Scope 1 and Scope 2.
- Methodology: Calculations follow the GHG Protocol using a control approach (operational control). Certain calculations are performed by a third party.
- Scope 1: Emissions from employee rental/leased cars only; total 67 t CO2e in 2024. Calculations based on total mileage in leasing agreements, converted to litres and kWh using average fuel/electricity per km. Fuel emission factors from DEFRA (2024) and the Norwegian Environment Agency; electricity factor from IEA (2024). Hybrid vehicles use combined fuel and electricity factors; electricity for hybrids/EVs is reported under Scope 2.
- Scope 2: Indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heating, and cooling; reported using both location-based and market-based methods.
- Location-based results (2024): Total Scope 2 emissions 1,379 t CO2e; electricity is the primary source at 1,247 t CO2e. Data primarily from activity data; estimates used for smaller Norwegian locations (based on other offices’ consumption) and international representative offices (using Odyssee-Mure per-employee statistics). Emission factors are country/region-based from IEA (2024).
text:
Location-based method
When using the location-based method, DNB’s total 
Scope 2 emissions were 1 379 t CO2e in 2024. Electricity 
was the most important source of Scope 2 emissions, 
with 1 247 t CO2e. Electricity was mainly reported using 
activity data, but for some of the smaller locations in 
Norway and the international representative offices, the 
consumption was estimated. For the locations in Norway, 
the estimates are based on consumption from other 
offices, and for the representative offices, the estimates 
are based on statistics on electricity consumption per 
employee from Odyssee-Mure. The emissions factors that 
were used for all electricity consumption under Scope 2 
are country- or region-based factors from the IEA in 
2024.

title: Market-based method
heading: 3.12.1.2.2 Market-based method
start_phrase: When using the market-based method, DNB’s total Scope 2 emissions were 384 t CO2e in 2024.
summary:
- The section explains DNB’s Scope 2 accounting under the market-based method for 2024, reporting total Scope 2 emissions of 384 t CO2e.
- Office electricity emissions are 0 t CO2e because DNB purchases guarantees of origin (GOs) covering 100% of its electricity consumption, making market-based emissions significantly lower than location-based results.
- A 2024 list shows 100% GO coverage across multiple countries; some GOs are bundled (Finland, UK, Sweden, Poland) and others unbundled (USA, Denmark, Latvia, Singapore, Chile, Luxembourg, China, Germany, Greece, Brazil, India, Spain, Australia, Switzerland).
- DNB does not buy GOs for electricity used by hybrid/electric cars or for district heating and cooling; these are calculated using the residual mix, which is typically higher than location-based factors due to Norway’s large export of GOs, implying more fossil-intensive electricity in the remaining mix.
- Consequently, emissions for these non-GO-covered energy uses are higher than under the location-based method.
- For Scope 3, financed emissions (category 15) are reported in CO2e, except for the shipping portfolio, which is reported in CO2 in line with IMO definitions.
text:
Market-based method 
When using the market-based method, DNB’s total Scope 2 
emissions were 384 t CO2e in 2024. In the market-
based method, the emissions associated with electricity 
consumption in office locations are 0 t CO2e, as a result 
of DNB buying guarantees of origin (GO) for renewable 
energy production for all of the electricity consumption. 
Emissions are therefore considerably lower when using 
this method than when using the location-based method.

title: Scope 3 - Introduction
heading: 3.12.1.3 Scope 3
start_phrase: Financed emissions in Scope 3, category 15, are reported in CO2 equivalents (CO2e), with the exception of the emissions in DNB’s shipping portfolio, which are reported in CO2, as this is clearly defined by the IMO and in the Poseidon Principles.
summary: Overview of DNB Group’s Scope 3, category 15 financed emissions reporting (ESRS E1), stating portfolio-level emissions are reported in CO2e except shipping, which is in CO2 per IMO/Poseidon Principles. Financed emissions equal DNB’s proportional share of client/investee emissions; due to varying company GHG scopes and gases, DNB uses CO2e and cannot detail gases per company. Reporting delimitations: loan portfolio coverage limited to sectors in the transition plan; customers’ Scope 3 not reported except for the oil and gas sector and DAM’s financed emissions, aligned with transition plan targets. Total reported emissions are 25,515,575 tonnes CO2e, comprising 85% actual data and 15% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2). For real estate portfolios (mortgages, commercial real estate, housing cooperatives), emissions factors use 2023 statistics from Norwegian authorities and sources (NVE, Norwegian Environment Agency, Norsk Energi, CEMAsys, Statistics Norway, fjernkontrollen.no), with an energy mix of district heating, electricity, oil, LPG/ethane, biofuels, and natural gas; year-to-year variability in the mix and carrier factors can materially change calculated financed emissions, and mixes differ between residential and commercial properties.
text:
Scope 3
Financed emissions in Scope 3, category 15, are reported 
in CO2 equivalents (CO2e), with the exception of the 
emissions in DNB’s shipping portfolio, which are reported 
in CO2, as this is clearly defined by the IMO and in the 
125
DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Environmental information  > ESRS E1 Climate change
Poseidon Principles. As DNB is a financial institution, 
the Group’s financed emissions are the sum of DNB’s 
proportion of emissions from the companies the Group 
finances and invests in. The companies’ greenhouse gas 
reporting varies in scope, and there are differences in 
the greenhouse gases that are included. This is why DNB 
has chosen CO2e as the relevant metric for emissions 
at portfolio level. The Group cannot provide a detailed 
overview of the gases that are included in the reporting 
for each company. 
Some delimitations have also been made for category 15: 
1. For the loan portfolio, the reporting is based on the 
sectors that are covered by the transition plan. 
2. DNB does not report on the customers’ Scope 3 
emissions, with the exception of the oil and gas sector 
and DAM’s financed emissions. The reporting covers 
the same emissions associated with the targets in the 
transition plan.
Of the emissions of 25 515 575 tonnes of CO2e 
that have been reported, 15 per cent were estimates 
and 85 per cent were actual data (ESRS 2 BP-2). The 
methodology for calculating greenhouse gas emissions 
for the various sectors is explained below.
For the real estate portfolios (mortgages, commercial 
real estate and housing cooperatives), the emissions 
factor used in the calculations is based on the last 
statistics available from the Norwegian Water Resources 
and Energy Directorate, the Norwegian Environment 
Agency, Norsk Energi, CEMAsys, Statistics Norway and 
fjernkontrollen.no  (a service from the trade association 
Norsk Fjernvarme), which are statistics from 2023. The 
energy mix used in the calculations consists of several 
different energy carriers: district heating, electricity, oil, 
LPG and ethane, biofuels and natural gas. The energy 
mix changes every year, and the same applies to the 
emissions factor for each energy carrier. The total 
emissions factor that is used to calculate DNB’s financed 
emissions may therefore change considerably from one 
year to the next, based on changes in the energy mix and 
underlying emissions factors. The energy mix also differs 
for the various real estate portfolios, considering that a 
home normally uses fewer different energy carriers than, 
for example, a commercial building.

title: Commercial real estate
heading: 3.12.1.3.1 Commercial real estate
start_phrase: The method for calculating absolute emissions from the commercial real estate portfolio is based on a methodology prepared by PCAF.
summary:
- Context: Excerpt from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report (ESRS E1 – Climate change) referencing the Poseidon Principles and focusing on financed emissions methodology.
- Financed emissions approach: As a financial institution, DNB reports its share of client companies’ emissions, using CO2e at portfolio level due to varying scopes and gases reported by clients; cannot provide gas-by-gas detail per company.
- Scope and delimitations (Category 15 – Investments): 
  - Loan portfolio reporting limited to sectors covered by DNB’s transition plan.
  - Customers’ Scope 3 not reported, except for oil and gas and DNB Asset Management’s financed emissions, aligned with transition plan targets.
- Data quality: Total reported financed emissions are 25,515,575 tCO2e, with 85% actual data and 15% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- Real estate portfolios (mortgages, commercial real estate, housing cooperatives): 
  - Emission factors sourced from Norwegian authorities and databases (NVE, Environment Agency, Norsk Energi, CEMAsys, Statistics Norway, fjernkontrollen.no), using 2023 statistics.
  - Energy carriers include district heating, electricity, oil, LPG/ethane, biofuels, natural gas; annual changes in energy mix and factors can materially affect financed emissions; mixes differ between residential and commercial assets.
- Commercial real estate methodology (PCAF-aligned):
  - Financed emissions = attribution factor (loan amount drawn/market value; using latest registered value rather than origination) × building emissions.
  - Building emissions = estimated energy consumption × emissions factor.
  - Energy consumption data sources:
    - EPC labels A–G where available (PCAF score 3.0), using Enova’s rating scale and median thresholds per class and building category.
    - CRREM national energy statistics (2020 baseline) to align with a 2050 net-zero pathway, with two sub-cases:
      - Area from Eiendomsverdi available (PCAF score 4.0): m2 × estimated kWh/m2.
      - Area not available (PCAF score 5.0): use portfolio average area as a standard value.
- Mortgages methodology:
  - Uses outstanding loan amount to apportion exposure to property-related emissions.
  - If property type is missing, defaults to “row house” as a conservative assumption that increases estimated energy consumption.
text:
Commercial real estate 
The method for calculating absolute emissions from 
the commercial real estate portfolio is based on a 
methodology prepared by PCAF. Financed emissions are 
calculated based on the loan-to-value ratio (loan amount drawn divided by market value, called an attribution 
factor), multiplied by emissions per building. Emissions 
per building are calculated based on the estimated 
energy consumption per building multiplied by an 
emissions factor. 
According to the PCAF methodology, the loan amount 
divided by the market value when the loan was 
established (at origination) is to be used. DNB has not 
registered this value, and the last market value registered 
is therefore used. 
The portfolio has two main sources for calculating energy 
consumption, divided as follows: 
 →EPC labels A–G are available (PCAF score 3.0): DNB 
uses Enova’s energy rating scale and calculates the 
average energy consumption (kWh/m2), based on 
calculation of the median between the threshold 
values per energy class. Enova’s energy rating scale 
per building category is linked to DNB’s sub-segments 
within commercial real estate. 
 →National energy statistics from CRREM’s database 
that show DNB’s best estimate in kWh/m2 per building 
and per country for 2020 (average figures per 
building category): The database must be used as a 
foundation for the trajectory to net-zero emissions in 
2050 (Pathway to 2050), and has been designed as 
an industry standard for commercial real estate. This 
category is divided into two sub-categories: 
 →DNB has retrieved the area in m2 from the real 
estate database Eiendomsverdi (PCAF score 
4.0): the area in m2 is multiplied by the estimated 
energy consumption per m2. 
 →DNB has not retrieved the area in m2 from the real 
estate database Eiendomsverdi (PCAF score 5.0): 
DNB uses the average area from the portfolio 
where the Group has the area as a standard value 
for the buildings the Group does not have data 
on.

title: Mortgages
heading: 3.12.1.3.2 Mortgages
start_phrase: The mortgage portfolio covers the properties that DNB’s personal customers have provided as collateral for their mortgages.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Outlines DNB’s approach to measuring financed emissions under ESRS E1, referencing the Poseidon Principles and using CO2e as the portfolio-level metric due to varying company GHG scopes and gases.
- Boundary choices (Scope 3, category 15 – Investments):
  - Loan portfolio reporting limited to sectors covered by DNB’s transition plan.
  - Customer Scope 3 emissions are not reported except for the oil and gas sector and DNB Asset Management’s financed emissions, aligned with transition plan targets.
- Data quality and coverage: Reports 25,515,575 tonnes CO2e; 85% based on actual data and 15% on estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2). DNB cannot provide a detailed gas-level breakdown per company.
- Real estate portfolios (mortgages, commercial real estate, housing cooperatives):
  - Emission factors built from latest Norwegian sources (NVE, Environment Agency, Norsk Energi, CEMAsys, Statistics Norway, fjernkontrollen.no), reflecting an annually changing energy mix (district heating, electricity, oil, LPG/ethane, biofuels, natural gas). Differences in portfolio energy mixes drive year-to-year variation.
- Commercial real estate methodology:
  - PCAF-based attribution using loan-to-value (amount drawn/market value) multiplied by building emissions; last registered market value used (origination value unavailable).
  - Energy use per building from:
    - EPC labels A–G via Enova’s scale (PCAF score 3.0), using median between class thresholds.
    - CRREM national energy statistics (Pathway to 2050) with two data-quality paths:
      - Area from Eiendomsverdi (PCAF 4.0).
      - No area; use portfolio average area proxy (PCAF 5.0).
- Mortgages methodology:
  - Exposure based on outstanding loan amount tied to collateral properties.
  - Conservative assumptions: default property type “row house” if unknown; use primary-room area when available, else gross area; for interval-based area data, take the upper bound.
  - EPC-to-energy conversion via Enova: A at 95% of A threshold value; B–F as averages with preceding class; G at 115% of F. Data quality targeted at PCAF score ~4.0 using internal EPC-covered reference sets.
- Housing cooperatives methodology:
  - PCAF-based attribution: joint debt/value of underlying homes; single attribution factor per cooperative; last Eiendomsverdi market value used.
  - Three data-quality scenarios:
    - ≥50% units with EPC labels and area derivable (PCAF 3.0) using Enova’s scale.
    - <50% EPC coverage but at least one known unit area (PCAF 4.0); apply known EPC as proxy for whole cooperative and infer total area.
    - No EPC and no area (PCAF 5.0); estimate EPC and area from similar-data subsets by housing type.
  - Housing type rules: “flat” if specified; if unknown, assign “row house.” Apply Enova area correction using either average corrections by housing type or unit counts when available. Use average attribution factor when key values are missing.
- Motor vehicles portfolio:
  - Covers on-balance credit exposures from DNB Finans across geographies, primarily passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, with assumptions on available vehicle data noted.
text:
Mortgages 
The mortgage portfolio covers the properties that 
DNB’s personal customers have provided as collateral 
for their mortgages. The outstanding loan amount for 
these mortgage agreements is used to calculate DNB’s 
exposure to emissions associated with these properties. 
For properties where DNB does not have information 
about the property type, the type ‘row house’ is assigned. 
This is a conservative approach, since row houses as 
an m2 correction means that the estimated energy 
consumption is higher.

 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Environmental information  > ESRS E1 Climate changeAccording to Enova’s conversion table, EPC label A means 
that the calculated energy delivered to the home per m2 
heated area (kWh/m2) is 95 per cent of the value listed 
for the A label. For EPC labels B to F, the energy delivered 
is calculated by taking the average of the relevant EPC 
label and the preceding EPC label. For EPC label G, the 
energy delivered is calculated as 115 per cent of F.
When DNB has information about the property type and 
area in m2, DNB’s portfolio is used to assign the property 
type an estimated consumption in kWh/m2. As a basis for 
the estimate, DNB uses an average of the consumption of 
the buildings in a separate portfolio that has coverage for 
EPC labels. This gives a score of 4 to 3 in DNB’s internal 
calculation model and counts towards a total PCAF score 
of 4.0. 
The calculation model chooses the value for primary 
rooms when this value is available. If this value is not 
available, the standard is to use gross area. As both of 
these are recorded in intervals, the highest value in the 
interval is used to ensure a conservative approach.

title: Housing cooperatives
heading: 3.12.1.3.3 Housing cooperatives
start_phrase: The sample for the calculations is DNB’s loans to housing cooperatives.
summary:
- Explains how Enova’s conversion table maps EPC labels to estimated energy delivered per m2: A set at 95% of the A threshold, B–F as the average of each label and the preceding one, and G at 115% of F.
- Describes DNB’s method to estimate kWh/m2 when property type and area are known, using averages from a portfolio with EPC coverage; contributes to an internal score and a total PCAF score of 4.0.
- States area selection rules: prefer primary rooms; if unavailable, use gross area; for interval data, use the upper bound for conservatism.
- Outlines PCAF-based financed emissions for housing cooperatives: emissions per building (estimated energy use × emissions factor) multiplied by an attribution factor; attribution is joint debt divided by the value of underlying homes; uses latest Eiendomsverdi market value when origination value is missing.
- Details three data-quality scenarios for housing cooperatives’ energy estimation:
  - ≥50% EPC coverage and some area data (PCAF 3.0): use Enova scale and median between class thresholds to derive kWh/m2 and total area.
  - <50% EPC coverage with minimal area data (PCAF 4.0): apply available EPC label(s) as proxy for the entire cooperative and extrapolate total area.
  - No EPC or area data (PCAF 5.0): estimate both EPC and area from the covered dataset within the same housing type.
- Specifies housing type handling: use “flat” if that is the only type in Eiendomsverdi; default to “row house” if unknown; acknowledges different Enova energy labels by type.
- Applies Enova’s area correction factor: estimate average correction by housing type when unit counts are unknown; when unit counts are known, apply correction per unit based on the Enova table; use an average attribution factor if property-specific values are missing.
- Introduces the motor vehicles portfolio scope: DNB Finans on-balance vehicle financing across geographies, primarily passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, with reporting assumptions noted.
text:
Housing cooperatives 
The sample for the calculations is DNB’s loans to housing 
cooperatives. The method for calculating absolute 
emissions is based on a methodology prepared by PCAF. 
Financed emissions are calculated based on the loan-to-
value ratio (loan amount drawn divided by market value, 
called an attribution factor), multiplied by emissions per 
building. The attribution factor for a housing cooperative 
is calculated based on the joint debt in the housing 
cooperative in question, divided by the value of the 
underlying homes in the housing cooperative. This means 
that DNB calculates a single attribution factor for housing 
cooperatives, while the attribution factor for mortgages is 
calculated based on the borrowing per underlying home. 
The emissions per building are calculated based on the 
estimated energy consumption per building multiplied by 
an emissions factor. According to the PCAF methodology, 
the amount drawn divided by the market value when the 
loan was established (at origination) is used. DNB has not 
registered this value, and the last market value registered 
in Eiendomsverdi is therefore used. 
Housing cooperatives have three main sources for 
calculating energy consumption, divided as follows: 
 →EPC labels A–G are available for 50 per cent or more 
of the homes in the housing cooperative (PCAF score 
3.0): When DNB has information on the area of one 
or more units in a housing cooperative, this is used to calculate the total area of the housing cooperative. 
DNB also requires that housing cooperatives have 
a coverage of 50 per cent or more of the units with 
a known EPC label. The Group uses Enova’s rating 
scale and calculates the average energy consumption 
(kWh/m2), based on calculation of the median 
between the threshold values per energy class. 
 →EPC labels are available for less than 50 per cent of 
the homes in the housing cooperative and DNB has 
information on the area of one or more units (PCAF 
score 4.0): Here DNB uses the EPC label in the 
housing cooperative as a standard value for the whole 
cooperative, even though DNB may have information 
on the EPC label of less than 50 per cent of the units. 
Here DNB also only requires that one unit has a known 
area. DNB then uses this to calculate the total area for 
the housing cooperative.
 →EPC labels and area are not available (PCAF score 
5.0): When DNB does not have data on either the 
area or the EPC label of any of the units in a housing 
cooperative, the rest of the data set for which DNB 
has coverage is used as a basis for estimating both 
the area and the EPC label within a given housing 
type.
The housing type can range from multi-dwelling houses 
(flats) to row houses. These have different energy labels 
in Enova’s energy rating scale. DNB chooses the housing 
type flat when flat is the only housing type given in 
Eiendomsverdi. If the housing type is not known, the type 
‘row house’ is assigned.
Enova’s energy rating scale also includes an area 
correction factor. When DNB estimates kWh/m2 but lacks 
information on the number of units (flats) in a housing 
cooperative, DNB estimates the area correction based on 
the average area correction per housing type. When DNB 
estimates kWh/m2 and has information on the number of 
units, DNB also estimates the area correction by charting 
the estimated kWh/m2 in the Enova table and multiplying 
the area correction by the number of units. When DNB 
does not have any values for the property, the Group 
chooses an average attribution factor based on the data 
set for which DNB has this data.

title: Motor vehicles
heading: 3.12.1.3.4 Motor vehicles
start_phrase: The motor vehicle sector includes DNB’s on-balance credit exposures associated with financing products for motor vehicles from DNB Finans, and covers customers in all geographical locations.
summary:
- Explains how DNB estimates building energy use from EPC labels using Enova’s conversion table: A = 95% of A-threshold kWh/m2; B–F = average of current and preceding label; G = 115% of F. When property type and area are known, DNB assigns kWh/m2 from a benchmarked internal portfolio with EPC coverage. Area preference is primary rooms, else gross area; upper bound of recorded interval is used for conservatism. Data quality contributes to PCAF scoring.

- Details financed-emissions methodology for housing cooperatives using PCAF: emissions per building = estimated energy consumption × emissions factor; financed share via an attribution factor (drawn amount/market value). If origination LTV is missing, latest Eiendomsverdi market value is used. Three data-quality tiers:
  - PCAF 3.0: ≥50% of units with EPC labels and at least one unit area known; Enova scale used to derive average kWh/m2.
  - PCAF 4.0: <50% EPC coverage but at least one unit area known; use available EPC labels as proxy for the entire cooperative.
  - PCAF 5.0: No EPC or area data; estimate both from the covered dataset by housing type.
  Housing type defaults to “flat” when only that is listed; otherwise “row house” if unknown. Applies Enova area correction factors, estimating by average per housing type when unit counts are unknown. Uses an average attribution factor when specific property values are missing.

- Describes motor-vehicle financed-emissions methods (DNB Finans portfolio; PCAF with Finance Norway adjustments), prioritized by data availability:
  - Method 1a: Actual fuel transactions × fuel-specific emissions factors; mileage from odometer deltas.
  - Method 1b: WLTP CO2 and actual mileage with period and attribution factors.
  - Method 2a: WLTP CO2 with statistically derived mileage, plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 3a: No WLTP or mileage; use PCAF default 224 g CO2/km and national average mileage (11,883 km). Uses EU-average mileage for Danish/Finnish passenger cars and Nordic averages for vans; 2024 applied vehicle-, country-, and engine-specific emissions factors.

- Outlines upstream oil and gas financed-emissions calculation (PCAF with Finance Norway): emissions from audited reports or Rystad Energy; attribution factor = DNB loan commitment / enterprise value (debt + equity); portfolio emissions sum = customer emissions × attribution factor.

- Presents salmon farming financed-emissions approach (PCAF with Finance Norway): prefer customer-reported data; otherwise calculate Scope 1–3 using SINTEF emissions factors tied to production volumes and average customer intensity. Attribution factor for listed companies uses Bloomberg enterprise value; for unlisted, total debt + equity adjusted by replacing book value of licences with market value (from latest auction averages). Production volumes and financials sourced from company reports.
text:
Motor vehicles
The motor vehicle sector includes DNB’s on-balance 
credit exposures associated with financing products for 
motor vehicles from DNB Finans, and covers customers 
in all geographical locations. The portfolio covers 
passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, which 
make up most of the portfolio. One of the assumptions 
for the reporting is that DNB Finans has information about 
127
DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Environmental information  > ESRS E1 Climate changethe motor vehicle make, model and fuel type. DNB uses 
the PCAF methodology, with the addition of Finance 
Norway’s recommendations for using the PCAF standard 
for Norwegian conditions. The most accurate data, as 
defined by the PCAF standard, is used for each exposure.
Method 1a: Actual fuel consumption 
For each line in the transaction log, emissions are 
calculated by multiplying the fuel volume by the specific 
emissions factor for the relevant fuel type. In most 
cases, the vehicle should use the same fuel for each 
transaction, but by using this method, the exact emissions 
are calculated per transaction, and the emissions will be 
added up afterwards. The mileage is calculated by taking 
the last (valid) reported mileage and deducting the first 
(valid) reported mileage. 
Method 1b: WLTP 16 – actual mileage, known 
fuel type
The actual known mileage is used here, as well as the CO2 
emissions from public motor vehicle data, in addition to a 
period factor and an attribution factor. 
Method 2a: WLTP – no mileage data, known 
fuel type
To calculate the mileage, local statistics are used, as well 
as the CO2 emissions from public motor vehicle data, in 
addition to a period factor and an attribution factor. 
Method 3a: No WLTP data, no mileage data 
and estimated vehicle type
For motor vehicles where neither the actual mileage nor 
WLTP data are available, the folllowing is used: PCAF 
data for passenger car emissions: 224 g CO2/km, and the 
national average mileage for Norwegian passenger cars: 
11 883 km. 
The availability and quality of data on mileage in Denmark 
and Finland is poor. This is why the mileage for passenger 
cars in Denmark and Finland was set at an average EU 
value, while the mileage for vans in Denmark and Finland 
is set at the Nordic average.
I 2024, a range of different emissions factors was used to 
reflect the various vehicles in DNB’s portfolio, in terms of 
vehicle type, country of registration and engine type.

title: Oil and gas
heading: 3.12.1.3.5 Oil and gas
start_phrase: For DNB’s upstream oil and gas portfolio, absolute financed emissions are calculated in accordance with the PCAF guidance, with the addition of the recommendations from Finance Norway for using the PCAF standard for Norwegian conditions.
summary:
- Describes DNB’s approach to calculating financed emissions using the PCAF methodology adapted with Finance Norway guidance, across motor vehicles, upstream oil and gas, and salmon farming.
- Motor vehicles:
  - Method 1a: Transaction-level actual fuel consumption multiplied by fuel-specific emission factors; mileage from last minus first valid odometer readings.
  - Method 1b: WLTP-based using actual mileage and vehicle CO2 data plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 2a: WLTP-based without mileage; mileage estimated from local statistics plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 3a: No WLTP or mileage; uses PCAF generic factors (224 g CO2/km) and average national mileage (11,883 km). For Denmark and Finland, applies EU average mileage for passenger cars and Nordic average for vans due to poor data.
  - 2024 uses differentiated emission factors by vehicle type, registration country, and engine type.
- Upstream oil and gas:
  - Financed emissions follow PCAF; emissions sourced from audited customer reports or Rystad Energy.
  - Attribution factor = DNB loan commitment / company value; company value = total debt + total equity (from audited accounts).
  - Portfolio emissions are the sum of customer emissions multiplied by attribution factors.
- Salmon farming:
  - Uses PCAF with Finance Norway adaptations; prioritizes customer-reported emissions.
  - When unavailable, calculates Scope 1–3 using SINTEF 2022 emissions factors and average intensity applied to reported production volumes.
  - Attribution factor based on drawn exposure:
    - Listed: divided by company value from Bloomberg.
    - Unlisted: divided by total debt + equity, adjusting license book values to market values (from latest auction averages).
  - Data on balance sheets and production volumes sourced from customer financial reports.
- Context: Content appears in the DNB Group Annual Report 2024, ESRS E1 Climate change section.
text:
Oil and gas 
For DNB’s upstream oil and gas portfolio, absolute 
financed emissions are calculated in accordance 
16 Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure. A standardised test method used to measure fuel consumption, CO2 emissions and vehicle 
range. with the PCAF guidance, with the addition of the 
recommendations from Finance Norway for using the 
PCAF standard for Norwegian conditions. 
Financed emissions are calculated by using an emission 
value and an attribution factor. The emission values are 
retrieved either from the customers’ audited reporting or 
from a third party data provider (Rystad Energy). 
The attribution factor is calculated by dividing DNB’s 
loan commitment vis-à-vis a customer by the customer’s 
company value. The company value is calculated as the 
customer’s total debt plus total equity, retrieved from the 
audited accounts. 
DNB’s absolute financed emissions are achieved by 
multiplying the customer’s emissions by the attribution 
factor and then adding up these values for the portfolio.

title: Salmon farming
heading: 3.12.1.3.6 Salmon farming
start_phrase: For the salmon farming sector, DNB uses the PCAF methodology, with the addition of Finance Norway’s recommendations for using the PCAF standard for Norwegian conditions.
summary:
- Describes DNB’s approach to calculating financed emissions under the PCAF standard, adapted with Finance Norway guidance, within the ESRS E1 Climate Change context.
- Motor vehicles methodology:
  - Uses the most accurate available data per exposure (make, model, fuel type).
  - Method 1a: Calculates emissions from actual fuel volume per transaction using fuel-specific factors; mileage from reported odometer readings.
  - Method 1b: Uses WLTP CO2 values with actual mileage, plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 2a: Uses WLTP CO2 values with estimated mileage from local statistics, plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 3a: Fallback with no WLTP or mileage: PCAF default 224 g CO2/km and Norwegian average 11,883 km.
  - Applies EU average mileage for passenger cars and Nordic average for vans in Denmark and Finland due to poor mileage data; in 2024 used differentiated emission factors by vehicle type, country, and engine type.
- Oil and gas (upstream) methodology:
  - Calculates absolute financed emissions per PCAF with Finance Norway adaptations.
  - Emissions sourced from audited customer reports or Rystad Energy.
  - Attribution factor = DNB loan commitment / company value (total debt + equity from audited accounts).
  - Portfolio emissions are the sum of customer emissions multiplied by the attribution factor.
- Salmon farming methodology:
  - Applies PCAF with Finance Norway adaptations.
  - Uses customer-reported emissions when available; otherwise estimates Scope 1–3 using SINTEF (2022) emissions factors and average intensity tied to production volumes.
  - Attribution factor based on DNB’s drawn exposure:
    - Listed companies: divides by company value (from Bloomberg).
    - Unlisted: divides by total debt + equity, adjusted by replacing on-balance licence values with market values (average of last auction round).
  - Financial and production data sourced from customer reports reviewed by credit analysts.
- Notes WLTP as the standardized test for vehicle fuel consumption, CO2 emissions, and range.
text:
Salmon farming 
For the salmon farming sector, DNB uses the PCAF 
methodology, with the addition of Finance Norway’s 
recommendations for using the PCAF standard for 
Norwegian conditions.
This is a sector where a number of customers report 
emission figures. Customer-reported emissions data 
is used where this is available. When it is not available, 
DNB calculates Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions by using 
a combination of emissions factors from the SINTEF 
report Greenhouse gas emissions of Norwegian salmon 
products  from 2022, and the average emissions intensity 
from DNB’s customers. These emissions factors are 
associated with production volume and are applied to the 
customers’ production volumes from their annual reports.
The attribution factor is calculated by dividing DNB’s 
drawn exposure towards the customer either by the 
company’s value if the customer is listed, or by the 
combined value of total debt and equity minus the on-
balance value of any licences, plus the market value of 
these licences if the customer is not listed.
For listed companies, the company’s value is obtained 
from Bloomberg, while the balance sheet value and the 
production volumes are obtained by a credit analyst from 
the customers’ financial reports. When the on-balance 
value of licences is replaced by the market value of the 
licences, the market value is calculated as the average 
price in the last auction round.

title: Steel
heading: 3.12.1.3.7 Steel
start_phrase: The steel sector includes DNB’s on-balance exposures towards customers in steel manufacturing in all geographical locations.
summary:
- Scope and methodology overview across sectors for DNB’s financed and operational emissions within the ESRS E1 Climate change context.
- Steel:
  - Covers on-balance exposures to steel manufacturing globally; excludes off-balance items.
  - Uses PCAF methodology adapted with Finance Norway’s guidance.
  - Prioritizes most accurate data per PCAF; for aluminium and steel customers in DNB’s transition plan, uses customer-reported emissions from the latest annual reports.
- Power generation:
  - Includes on-balance credit exposures globally; excludes off-balance.
  - Applies PCAF with Finance Norway recommendations and most accurate data per exposure.
  - Obtains reported emissions or production volumes from customers; uses extrapolation where data is missing to achieve full coverage.
- DNB Næringseiendom (real estate):
  - Monitors energy via Optima; calculations follow the GHG Protocol.
  - Location-based Scope 2 approach using Nordic electricity mix; guarantees of origin not factored.
  - Emission factors: electricity from CEMAsys; district energy and local heating/cooling from suppliers/Entro.
  - Data primarily from electronic meters; reports only buildings with full, comparable year-over-year data; excludes planning-phase assets, high-vacancy buildings, or those not owned for the full year.
- DNB Livsforsikring (life insurance):
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research data for portfolio companies’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions; Scope 3 excluded.
  - Financed emissions reporting covers ~65% of the portfolio.
  - For listed equities and bonds, ~85% data coverage; remaining 15% imputed using the average emissions of companies with available data.
- DNB Asset Management (DAM):
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research; high coverage for equities, lower for fixed income, especially Nordic FI.
  - Portfolio carbon footprint weighted by holdings; cash allocated proportionally across holdings.
  - For missing company data, uses MSCI modelled estimates; if neither reported nor estimated data exist, applies an average of companies with reported data.
- Shipping:
  - Includes Scope 1 emissions for vessels ≥5,000 gross tonnes (aligned with IMO reporting threshold); excludes off-balance exposures.
  - Calculates absolute financed emissions using ship-level data: fuel type, fuel volume during the period, and emissions factors per fuel type, sourced from customers or a designated third party.
text:
Steel
The steel sector includes DNB’s on-balance exposures 
towards customers in steel manufacturing in all 
geographical locations. Off-balance exposures are not 
included. 
DNB uses the PCAF methodology, with the addition of 
Finance Norway’s recommendations for using the PCAF 
standard for Norwegian conditions. The most accurate 
data, as defined by the PCAF standard, is used for each 
exposure. For all customers in aluminium and steel 
that are covered by the transition plan, DNB uses the 
customers’ reported emissions. These are obtained from 
the customers’ annual reports. DNB has used the last 
annual report and data available.

title: DNB Næringseiendom
heading: 3.12.1.3.9 DNB Næringseiendom
start_phrase: DNB Næringseiendom monitors energy consumption through the Optima energy and environmental monitoring system.
summary:
- Overview: Partial sustainability report detailing how DNB measures and reports financed emissions across key sectors using PCAF methodology supplemented by Finance Norway guidance, prioritizing the most accurate data per exposure and focusing on on-balance sheet exposures.

- Steel (and aluminium under transition plans): Uses PCAF with Finance Norway recommendations; relies on customers’ latest reported emissions from annual reports; on-balance exposures only.

- Power generation: On-balance credit exposures included; PCAF plus Finance Norway guidance; emissions or production data obtained directly from customers; extrapolation used where data is missing to achieve full coverage.

- DNB Næringseiendom (commercial real estate): Energy use monitored via the Optima system; calculations follow GHG Protocol with location-based Scope 2; Nordic electricity mix used without guarantees of origin; emission factors from CEMAsys (electricity) and suppliers/Entro (district/local energy); primary data from meters; reporting limited to buildings with full, comparable annual data (excludes planning phase, high vacancy, or not owned for full year).

text:
DNB Næringseiendom monitors energy consumption 
through the Optima energy and environmental monitoring 
system. The calculations follow the standard described 
in the GHG Protocol. All emissions are converted to CO2 
equivalents, and the location-based methodology reflects 
emissions from production of electricity distributed in 
the Nordic electricity network and does not factor in 
guarantees of origin. For direct electricity consumption, 
the Nordic electricity mix is used. The emissions factors 
are allocated to the various energy sources, with direct 
electricity coming from CEMAsys, while district cooling, 
district heating, local cooling and local heating come 
from energy suppliers and Entro. Direct electricity 
consumption represents most of DNB Næringseiendom’s 
Scope 2 emissions. Energy consumption data is primarily 
obtained electronically from meters.
Reporting is only provided for buildings with full data 
coverage and comparability from year to year. Buildings 
that are in the planning phase or that have a high vacancy rate, or that are not owned during the entire reporting 
year, are excluded.

title: DNB Livsforsikring
heading: 3.12.1.3.10 DNB Livsforsikring
start_phrase: DNB Livsforsikring uses data from MSCI ESG Research to measure the greenhouse gas emissions of the companies in its portfolios.
summary:
- Overview of sectoral financed-emissions methodologies across DNB’s portfolios, focusing on on-balance exposures only and excluding off-balance items.
- Consistent application of PCAF methodology supplemented by Finance Norway’s guidance, using the highest-quality data available per exposure.
- Steel (and aluminium under the transition plan): use of customers’ latest reported emissions from annual reports.
- Power generation: inclusion of all on-balance credit exposures; collection of customer-reported emissions or production volumes; extrapolation applied where data is missing.
- DNB Næringseiendom (real estate): energy and emissions monitored via Optima; calculations follow the GHG Protocol using location-based Scope 2; Nordic electricity mix for direct electricity; emission factors from CEMAsys, energy suppliers, and Entro; reporting limited to buildings with full, comparable data and excludes those under planning, with high vacancy, or not owned for the full year.
- DNB Livsforsikring: portfolio emissions measured with MSCI ESG Research data (Scope 1 and 2 only); financed-emissions reporting covers ~65% of the portfolio; ~85% data coverage for shares/bonds; missing data filled by assigning the average emissions of companies with data.
- DNB Asset Management (DAM): uses MSCI ESG Research; high coverage for equities, lower for fixed income (especially Nordic); carbon footprint weighted by portfolio holdings with cash allocated proportionally; uses MSCI modelled estimates where companies lack reported data, and portfolio averages where neither reported nor estimated data exist.
- Shipping: Scope 1 emissions for vessels ≥5,000 gross tonnes (aligned with IMO threshold); excludes off-balance exposures; absolute financed emissions calculated from ship-level fuel type, fuel volume, and fuel-specific emission factors.
text:
DNB Livsforsikring uses data from MSCI ESG Research to 
measure the greenhouse gas emissions of the companies 
in its portfolios. The emissions are based on Scope 1 
and 2 emissions. Indirect emissions (Scope 3 emissions) 
associated with purchased goods and services, as 
well as use and disposal of products, are not included. 
The reporting on financed emissions covers about 
65 per cent of DNB Livsforsikring’s portfolio. For shares 
and bonds, the company has a data coverage of about 
85 per cent. In order to compensate for a lack of data for 
the remaining 15 per cent, DNB Livsforsikring assigns the 
same emissions value to these companies as the average 
of the companies for which DNB Livsforsikring has data.

title: DNB Asset Management
heading: 3.12.1.3.11 DNB Asset Management
start_phrase: DAM uses data from MSCI ESG Research to measure the greenhouse gas emissions of the companies in its portfolio.
summary:
- Document focus: How DNB measures and reports financed and operational greenhouse gas emissions across key portfolios under ESRS E1, including methodologies, data sources, scope, and data coverage/assumptions.
- Common approach: Prioritizes on-balance exposures; applies PCAF methodology with Finance Norway adaptations where relevant; uses the most accurate data available per exposure; relies on customer-reported data when possible and applies estimation/extrapolation for gaps.

- Steel:
  - Scope: On-balance exposures in steel manufacturing globally; off-balance excluded.
  - Method: PCAF + Finance Norway guidance.
  - Data: Customer-reported emissions from the latest annual reports; uses most accurate data per PCAF.

- Power generation:
  - Scope: On-balance credit exposures globally; off-balance excluded.
  - Method: PCAF + Finance Norway guidance.
  - Data: Customer-reported emissions or production volumes; extrapolation used where data are missing to achieve full coverage.

- DNB Næringseiendom (real estate):
  - Monitoring: Optima energy and environmental system.
  - Method: GHG Protocol; CO2e conversion; location-based Scope 2 using Nordic electricity mix (no guarantees of origin).
  - Emission factors: Electricity from CEMAsys; district heating/cooling and local heating/cooling from suppliers and Entro.
  - Data capture: Primarily electronic meter data.
  - Reporting boundary: Only buildings with full, comparable year-over-year data; excludes planning-phase assets, high-vacancy buildings, and assets not owned for the full year.

- DNB Livsforsikring:
  - Data source: MSCI ESG Research.
  - Scope: Financed emissions based on Scope 1 and 2 only (Scope 3 excluded).
  - Coverage: ~65% of total portfolio; ~85% for shares and bonds.
  - Estimation: For the remaining ~15%, assigns the portfolio average emissions of companies with data.

- DNB Asset Management (DAM):
  - Data source: MSCI ESG Research.
  - Coverage: High for equities; lower for fixed income, especially Nordic fixed income.
  - Method: Holdings-weighted portfolio carbon footprint; cash allocated proportionally.
  - Estimation: Uses MSCI modelled estimates where company data are missing; if neither reported nor modelled data exist, applies the average of companies with reported data.

- Shipping:
  - Scope: Scope 1 emissions for vessels ≥5,000 GT (aligned with IMO threshold); off-balance excluded.
  - Method: Absolute financed emissions calculated using ship-level data:
    - Fuel type
    - Fuel volume consumed
    - Emission factors per fuel type
text:
DNB Asset Management 
DAM uses data from MSCI ESG Research to measure 
the greenhouse gas emissions of the companies in 
its portfolio. The coverage for the share portfolio is 
fairly high, but it is a little lower for the fixed-income 
instruments, and unfortunately the coverage of the 
carbon emissions for the Nordic fixed-income market is 
low. 
The companies’ carbon footprint is weighted 
according to the respective holdings in the portfolios. 
In the calculations, cash in the portfolios is allocated 
proportionally between the other companies. For 
companies without reported emissions data, MSCI ESG 
Research produces modelled estimates that are used 
in the calculation. In addition, some companies have 
neither reported nor estimated data. In such cases, DAM 
calculates a figure for the company based on the average 
of the companies with reported data.

title: Shipping
heading: 3.12.1.3.12 Shipping
start_phrase: The shipping portfolio includes Scope 1 emissions for vessels of 5 000 gross tonnes or more.
summary:
- Sector methodologies for financed emissions:
  - Steel: On-balance exposures only; PCAF methodology with Finance Norway adaptations; use most accurate data per exposure; for aluminium and steel clients in DNB’s transition plan, use customers’ reported emissions from latest annual reports.
  - Power generation: On-balance exposures only; PCAF with Finance Norway guidance; collect reported emissions/production directly from customers; extrapolate where data is missing to achieve full coverage.

- Real estate (DNB Næringseiendom):
  - Energy and emissions monitored via Optima; calculations follow GHG Protocol.
  - Location-based approach using Nordic electricity mix; emission factors from CEMAsys (electricity) and suppliers/Entro (district cooling/heating, local systems).
  - Direct electricity is the main Scope 2 source; metered electronic data.
  - Reporting limited to buildings with complete, comparable annual data; excludes planning-phase assets, high-vacancy buildings, and those not owned for the full year.

- Insurance (DNB Livsforsikring):
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research for portfolio emissions (Scope 1 and 2 only; excludes Scope 3).
  - Financed emissions reporting covers ~65% of portfolio; ~85% coverage for shares and bonds.
  - For remaining 15% with no data, assigns average emissions of covered companies.

- Asset management (DNB Asset Management):
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research; higher coverage for equities than fixed income, with low coverage in Nordic fixed income.
  - Portfolio carbon footprint is holdings-weighted; cash allocated proportionally.
  - Uses MSCI modelled estimates when company data is missing; if neither reported nor estimated data exist, applies portfolio average.

- Shipping portfolio:
  - Includes Scope 1 for vessels ≥5,000 GT (IMO threshold); off-balance exposures excluded.
  - Absolute financed emissions computed from fuel type/volume and standard emission factors (IMO/Poseidon Principles).
  - Attribution factor = DNB lending exposure / ship’s year-end market value; applied to ship emissions and aggregated across portfolio.

- Greenhouse gas intensity based on net revenue:
  - Defined as total tCO2e divided by net revenue (sum of net interest income and net other operating income; NOK 86,537 million in 2024).
  - 2024 intensity: 0.0003 tCO2e/NOK for both location- and market-based; no prior-year comparative provided.

- Climate credits:
  - Strategic focus on real-economy emissions reductions; credits considered for hard-to-abate residuals long term.
  - For own operations, credits purchased annually since 2014 for measured Scope 1 and selected Scope 3 (e.g., travel, waste); 7,088 tCO2e purchased in 2024 via klimate.co with rigorous due diligence.
  - Projects are 100% carbon storage: biosphere (ecosystem restoration, soil carbon) and geosphere (DACCS, mineralization).
  - Verified against Plan (46.5%), Gold Standard (34%), Artisanal C‑Sink (5%), Verra VCS (14%), EBC C‑Sink (0.5%); 99.6% outside Europe; credits annulled 2017–2024.
  - Intention to continue decarbonising operations to reduce reliance on credits.

Shipping 
The shipping portfolio includes Scope 1 emissions for 
vessels of 5 000 gross tonnes or more. This threshold is 
the same as the reporting threshold used by the IMO. 
Off-balance exposures are not included. 
Absolute financed emissions for DNB’s shipping portfolio 
are calculated as follows: First DNB obtains the following 
data points for each ship, either directly from the customer 
or through a third party that acts on behalf of DNB:
 →fuel type
 →fuel volume consumed during the period
 →emissions factors per fuel type
