multiplied by the corresponding fuel-specific emissions 
factor to calculate the emissions from the ship in question 
for a given period. The emissions factors are the industry 
standard and are used by the IMO and in the Poseidon 
Principles.
In order to determine DNB’s proportion of a ship’s 
emissions, an attribution factor is calculated by dividing 
DNB’s lending exposure by the ship’s last available 
market value at year-end. This attribution factor is then 
multiplied by the ship’s emissions in order to calculate 
DNB’s proportion of the ship’s emissions. This process 
is repeated for each ship in DNB’s portfolio, and these 
proportions are then added up to give the total absolute 
financed emissions for DNB’s shipping portfolio.

title: Greenhouse gas intensity based on net income
heading: 3.12.2 Greenhouse gas intensity based on net income
start_phrase: The greenhouse gas intensity is calculated by dividing total greenhouse gas emissions in tonnes of CO2e by net revenue in NOK.
summary:
- Explains how financed emissions from DNB’s shipping portfolio are calculated: ship-level emissions are derived by multiplying fuel consumption by standard, fuel-specific emission factors (aligned with IMO and Poseidon Principles). DNB’s share is attributed by dividing its lending exposure by each ship’s year-end market value and multiplying by the ship’s emissions; results are aggregated across the portfolio to obtain total absolute financed emissions.
- Defines greenhouse gas intensity based on net revenue: total GHG emissions (tCO2e) divided by net revenue (NOK). For 2024, both location-based and market-based intensities are 0.0003 tCO2e/NOK; comparative data are not available. Net revenue equals Net interest income plus Net other operating income (NOK 86,537 million).
- Details DNB’s approach to climate credits under ESRS E1-7: prioritizes real-economy emissions reductions, viewing carbon credits as a long-term tool for residual emissions. For own operations, DNB has purchased credits for measured Scope 1 and upstream/own-operations Scope 3 emissions since 2014; in 2024 it bought 7,088 tCO2e of credits.
- Credits were sourced via klimate.co with rigorous due diligence (300+ data points) and are 100% carbon storage, focused on carbon removal in the biosphere (e.g., ecosystem restoration, soil carbon) and geosphere (e.g., DACCS, mineralization). Verification standards include Plan (46.5%), Gold Standard (34%), Verra VCS (14%), Artisanal C-Sink (5%), and EBC C-Sink (0.5%); 99.6% of projects are outside Europe. Credits were annulled during 2017–2024. DNB aims to continue decarbonizing operations to minimize reliance on credits.

title: Purchase of climate credits
heading: 3.12.3 Purchase of climate credits
start_phrase: Achieving the net-zero ambition will require that both DNB and its customers continue to increase the pace of emissions reduction associated with the real economy.
summary:
- Methodology for financed shipping emissions: Ship emissions are calculated by multiplying each fuel type consumed by its industry-standard emissions factor (as used by IMO and the Poseidon Principles).
- Attribution of financed emissions: DNB’s share of a ship’s emissions is determined by an attribution factor (DNB lending exposure divided by the ship’s last available year-end market value), applied to the ship’s emissions; summed across all ships to obtain total absolute financed emissions for the shipping portfolio.
- Greenhouse gas intensity metric: GHG intensity is total emissions (tCO2e) divided by net revenue (NOK).
- Reported GHG intensity: Both location-based and market-based emissions per net revenue are 0.0003 tCO2e/NOK for 2024; comparative figures are not available.
- Revenue basis: Net revenue equals Net interest income plus Net other operating income (NOK 86,537 million; per Group income statement).
- Carbon credits strategy: Primary focus is on enabling real-economy emissions reductions; credits are considered for hard-to-abate residual emissions over the long term.
- 2024 carbon credit purchases: DNB purchased 7,088 tCO2e in credits for measured direct and indirect emissions in own operations and upstream value chain (Scopes 1 and 3), continuing a practice since 2014.
- Vendor and due diligence: Credits bought from klimate.co, which assesses projects using 300+ data points on climate impact, additionality, integrity, and prospects.
- Nature of projects: 100% carbon storage via biosphere removals (e.g., ecosystem restoration, soil carbon) and geosphere removals (e.g., DACCS, mineralization).
- Standards and distribution: Projects verified under Plan (46.5%), Gold Standard (34%), Verra VCS (14%), Artisanal C-Sink (5%), EBC C-Sink (0.5%); 99.6% located outside Europe.
- Retirement of credits: Credits annulled over 2017–2024.
- Ongoing commitment: DNB aims to further decarbonise operations to avoid reliance on carbon credits.
text:
Purchase of climate credits
ESRS E1-7 Projects relating to removal of greenhouse gases 
and limitation of greenhouse gas emissions financed using 
climate quotas
Achieving the net-zero ambition will require that 
both DNB and its customers continue to increase the 
pace of emissions reduction associated with the real 
economy. In light of this, the Group’s main focus is on 
enabling considerable emissions reductions, and not 
on using carbon credits in the short term. However, 
DNB acknowledges that in the long term it will be more 
difficult to eliminate emissions from some activities, and 
that carbon credits represent a possible solution for these 
residual emissions. In relation to own operations, DNB has bought carbon 
credits for all present, measured direct and indirect 
emissions (for example from air travel and waste 
management) associated with the upstream value 
chain and own operations (Scope 1 and 3) since 2014. 
DNB has also done this for 2024, and in total bought 
7 088 t CO2e in carbon credits at the end of the year. 
The carbon credits were bought from klimate.co, which 
carries out a thorough due diligence assessment of all 
projects to ensure quality and integrity. The company 
collects over 300 data points on climate effects, 
additional effects, integrity and future prospects for 
each project. The projects that have been purchased 
involve 100 per cent carbon storage, and are associated 
with carbon removal to both the biosphere and to the 
geosphere. Carbon removal to the biosphere entails 
increasing the amount of carbon stored in the biosphere, 
for example by restoring healthy ecosystems (for example 
woodlands, grasslands, wetlands and marine habitats) 
or increasing soil carbon in agricultural land. Carbon 
removal to the geosphere entails extracting CO2 from 
the atmosphere and storing it in the geosphere, for 
example through Direct Air Capture and Storage (DACCS) 
or by converting atmospheric carbon into rock through 
remineralisation. The projects that have been purchased 
have been verified against quality standards like Plan 
(46.5 per cent), Gold Standard (34 per cent), Artisanal 
C-Sink standard (5 per cent), Verra VCS (14 per cent) 
and EBC C-Sink (0.5 per cent). 99.6 per cent of the 
projects purchased are outside Europe. The carbon 
credits were annulled in the period 2017 to 2024. 
It is DNB’s intention to continue to decarbonise the 
Group’s operations so that the Group does not need to 
use carbon credits.

title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 4.1.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: In the materiality analysis, extraction and use of marine resources was identified as a risk for DNB, as well as an area in which the Group has an indirect impact.
summary:
- Focus area: ESRS E3 Water and marine resources, specifically the extraction and use of marine resources.
- Materiality: Identified as a material risk and area of indirect impact for DNB under ESRS 2 IRO-1 and ESRS 2 SBM-3. Relevance spans short, medium, and long term.
- Context: DNB mirrors Norway’s sea-based economy (oil and gas, offshore, seafood). Seafood is a major exposure in DNB’s portfolio; one-fourth of Norway’s value creation comes from the sea.
- Impact and risk drivers: Dependence on marine resources can negatively affect marine ecosystems, biodiversity, and local communities; resource reduction, degradation, or stricter regulation can cause income loss and higher costs for financed companies; reputational risks exist in oil and gas, fish farming, and other marine sectors.
- Management approach (ESRS E3-1):
  - Group policy for sustainability: Integrates climate, environmental, social, and governance considerations across all activities; commits to sustainable marine resource management, biodiversity promotion, and natural risk reduction; embedded in credit processes, risk assessments, and expectations documents.
  - Group instructions for sustainability in credit activities: Excludes financing for unregulated or unsustainable fishing practices (seabed-damaging gear, harmful techniques, endangered species fishing, drift nets >2.5 km) and fish farming without required permits; no financing for companies materially harming legally protected habitats.
- Cross-references: Further process and governance details provided under ESRS 2 General disclosures and ESRS E1.
text:
In the materiality analysis, extraction and use of marine 
resources was identified as a risk for DNB, as well as 
an area in which the Group has an indirect impact. See 
the discussion of the process to establish and assess 
material impacts, risks and opportunities relating to the 
topic water and marine resources under Process for 
double materiality assessment (ESRS 2 IRO-1) in the 
sub-chapter ESRS 2 General disclosures. DNB reflects 
the Norwegian economy, where sectors like oil and gas, 
offshore and seafood represent important industries. 
One-fourth of all value creation in Norway comes from the 
sea, and in DNB’s banking operations, seafood is one of 
the sectors that the Group has the greatest exposure to. 
Companies in the maritime sector both use and depend 
on marine resources. This can have a negative impact on 
the ecosystem and biodiversity of the sea, and on people 
in local communities that depend strongly on marine 
resources and business activities associated with the 
extraction of these. Reduction, degradation or stricter 
regulation of these resources can also lead to loss of 
income and increased costs for the companies financed 
by DNB. In addition, reputational risk is associated with 
investment in oil and gas, fish farming and other marine 
sectors. DNB therefore has a potential negative impact 
and risk associated with the extraction and use of marine 
resources through the companies the Group finances and 
invests in. The negative impact and the risk are equally 
relevant in the short, medium and long term. Managing impacts, risks and 
opportunities

title: Governing documents
heading: 4.1.2.1 Governing documents
start_phrase: In order to manage DNB’s risks and material impacts, several governing documents and methods have been prepared to provide guidance for how the Group is to contribute to sustainable management of marine resources and promote biodiversity and reduce natural risk.
summary:
- Scope: ESRS E3 Water and marine resources, with emphasis on extraction and use of marine resources.
- Materiality and strategy (ESRS 2 IRO-1, ESRS 2 SBM-3): Identified as a material risk and area of indirect impact for DNB due to Norway’s ocean-based economy (oil and gas, offshore, seafood). Highlights ecosystem and community impacts, regulatory and operational cost risks for financed companies, and reputational risk in oil and gas, aquaculture, and other marine sectors. Risks are relevant short, medium and long term.
- Governance and policies (ESRS E3-1): 
  - Group policy for sustainability embeds marine resource stewardship, biodiversity promotion and natural risk reduction across credit, investment, advisory, procurement and operations.
  - Group instructions for credit exclude financing of unregulated/unsustainable fishing (e.g., seabed-damaging gear, harmful techniques, endangered species, drift nets >2.5 km) and unpermitted fish farming; no financing for entities materially harming legally protected habitats. EVP Risk Management oversees adherence.
  - DNB Asset Management (DAM) expectations for investee aquaculture companies on sustainable practices, governance, strategy and KPI reporting.
- Processes and methods: 
  - Corporate customers with commitments > NOK 50 million assessed for environmental management systems, supplier oversight, and absence of recent environmental fines; non-compliance triggers follow-up.
  - DAM designates sea/aquaculture as a responsible investment focus, conducts ownership dialogues, and votes to promote sustainable aquaculture.
  - Collaboration with peers via FAIRR (ESG risks in food sector) and UNEP FI’s Sustainable Blue Economy Finance Initiative.
- Actions and resources (ESRS E3-2): Topic deemed material in 2024; no ESRS E3-compliant measures implemented yet. DNB is collecting data and stakeholder input to establish meaningful metrics and targets. For 2025, plans include an action plan with metrics on marine resource extraction/use and sector-specific customer follow-up targets; existing methods continue in the interim.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS E3-3): No specific targets set yet; focus on deepening understanding of impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities to ensure realistic, sector-appropriate targets. Effectiveness of policy compliance not directly measured; reliance on embedded methods in products and services.

Governing documents

title: Actions
heading: 4.1.2.2 Actions
start_phrase: The topic extraction and use of water and marine resources was identified as a material topic in 2024.
summary:
- Governance and accountability: The EVP of Risk Management oversees implementation of Group sustainability instructions in credit activities. DNB Asset Management (DAM) has issued an expectations document for investee companies on sustainable aquaculture, covering governance, strategy, and reporting on relevant KPIs.

- Risk assessment in lending: All corporate customers with commitments over NOK 50 million are assessed for environmental management systems, supplier environmental follow-up, and absence of environmental fines or reports in the past three years; noncompliant companies are followed up by customer teams.

- Responsible investment and stewardship: Sea and aquaculture are priority themes for DAM, which engages in ongoing ownership dialogues and votes at AGMs to advance sustainable aquaculture. DAM collaborates with peers via FAIRR and UNEP FI’s Sustainable Blue Economy Finance Initiative.

- Actions (ESRS E3-2): Extraction and use of water and marine resources were identified as material in 2024. While no ESRS E3-compliant measures had been implemented at the reporting date, DNB has begun collecting data and insights to set meaningful, measurable metrics and targets. For 2025, DNB plans an action plan with metrics on marine resource extraction/use and targets for customer follow-up, alongside existing methods already in use.

- Metrics and targets (ESRS E3-3): No specific targets have been set yet; DNB is developing its understanding of impacts, dependencies, risks, and opportunities related to marine resources. Targets will be realistic and sector-appropriate. DNB does not directly measure compliance effectiveness but uses various methods that incorporate marine resource considerations, with related policies referenced under ESRS E3-1.

heading: 5.1.1.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: DNB is a large employer with around 11 000 employees and has a direct impact on its own workforce.
summary:
- Focus area: ESRS S1 Own workforce, emphasizing diversity, gender equality, and equal pay for work of equal value under ESRS 2 SBM-3 (material impacts, risks, opportunities).
- Scope and scale: DNB’s own workforce includes ~11,000 permanent and temporary employees plus hired consultants, across all locations.
- Materiality: Diversity and equality identified as among the most material short‑term topics due to significant impacts and opportunities for the Group.
- Strategic ambition: Be a driving force for diversity and inclusion as part of sustainable value creation and ethical foundations.
- Business value: Advancing equal opportunities is expected to boost productivity, innovation, customer satisfaction, and talent attraction/retention.
- Priority focus: Gender balance in management and increased representation of multicultural backgrounds.
- Key measures: Establish a multicultural diversity network, embed diversity in hiring processes, and integrate D&I topics into leadership development (with additional activities referenced under ESRS S1-4).
- Coverage: Initiatives apply to the entire workforce, including international offices.
- Climate transition link: 2023 transition plan includes building employees’ climate and transition competence to support client advisory; related competence-building is referenced under ESRS E1-3 (Climate change).
- Governance and policies (ESRS S1-1): Code of Conduct, Group sustainability policy, and People Guide set expectations for equality, diversity, and inclusion; the Code of Conduct anchors the ambition to lead on these areas.
text:
DNB is a large employer with around 11 000 employees 
and has a direct impact on its own workforce. Own 
workforce means all permanent and temporary employees 
in DNB, as well as hired consultants (hereinafter referred 
to as own employees). 
In the assessment of the impacts, risks and opportunities 
for DNB associated with own employees, diversity, gender 
equality and equal pay for work of equal value (hereinafter 
referred to diversity and equality) were assessed as two 
of the topics where DNB has the greatest impact and 
opportunities. DNB can have a positive impact on its 
employees by creating equal opportunities and can also 
achieve increased value creation for the Group by working 
actively with diversity. The topics mentioned above were 
assessed as most material in the short term in the Group’s 
materiality analysis because this is something DNB must 
focus on here and now. 
One of DNB’s sustainability ambitions is to be a driving 
force for diversity and inclusion, which is part of DNB’s 
overall strategic ambition to deliver sustainable value 
creation. Having a diverse workforce and gender 
equality is consistent with DNB’s ethical foundation. The 
employees being different and reflecting society makes 
DNB better, and the Group therefore works to ensure that 
the employees have equal opportunities. By investing in 
the employees’ development and satisfaction through 
measures to improve diversity and equality, DNB can 
increase its productivity, innovative power and customer 
satisfaction. DNB places great emphasis on creating an 
inclusive and supportive working environment, which can 
help attract and retain talented employees. The Group 
has a special focus on gender balance in management positions. In addition, having employees with a 
multicultural background is a priority area in the strategy 
for diversity and inclusion. 
The measures to strengthen the positive impacts 
and opportunities include establishing a network for 
multicultural diversity, focusing on diversity in employment 
processes and integrating the topics of diversity and 
inclusion in leadership development programmes. Several 
activities are described under Actions (ESRS S1-4). 
The goal is to create a better working environment and 
increase the employees’ engagement and productivity. 
DNB’s work with equality and diversity covers the entire 
workforce, including the international offices. 
In connection with DNB’s transition plan, which was 
launched in 2023, measures were also implemented 
to increase the employees’ climate and transition 
competence. DNB will use the employees’ competence 
to help customers in their transition through advisory 
services, among other things, and the transition plan thus 
provides a foundation for competence building measures 
for the employees. See the discussion of competence 
building associated with the climate and transition for own 
employees under Actions (ESRS E1-3) in the sub-chapter 
ESRS E1 Climate change.

title: Governing documents
heading: 5.1.1.2.1 Governing documents
start_phrase: DNB’s Code of Conduct, Group policy for sustainability and People Guide (the Employee Handbook) determine how the Group should work with diversity and equality.
summary:
- Scope and context: The section covers ESRS S1 for DNB’s own workforce (around 11,000 people), including permanent and temporary employees and hired consultants, across domestic and international operations.

- Materiality and strategy: Diversity, gender equality and equal pay for work of equal value are identified as short‑term, most material topics with significant impacts, risks and opportunities. A diverse and inclusive workforce is positioned as core to DNB’s ethical foundation and sustainable value creation, enhancing productivity, innovation, customer satisfaction, talent attraction and retention.

- Strategic priorities and actions: Focus on gender balance in management and increased multicultural representation. Measures include a multicultural diversity network, integrating diversity and inclusion in leadership programs, and embedding diversity considerations in hiring processes. The 2023 transition plan adds employee climate and transition competence building to support client advisory, linked to ESRS E1.

- Governance and policies (ESRS S1‑1, ESRS 2 MDR‑P): The Code of Conduct, Group policy for sustainability, and the People Guide set expectations for equality, non‑discrimination and inclusion. The Code bans discrimination and harassment on multiple grounds, applies group‑wide (including consultants, Board members), and is Board‑approved. Operational responsibility rests with executives and managers, who ensure compliance and training.

- Controls and monitoring: Ongoing internal control over working environment and HSE compliance; annual confirmation that employees have read the Code; monitoring of diversity and discrimination via employee surveys; stakeholder involvement in policy updates (audit, second‑line functions, unions, governance). Documents are accessible internally and publicly.

- Human rights commitments: Alignment with UN human rights instruments and ILO core conventions; risk‑based review of DNB’s own value chain for human and labour rights risks, with measures per OECD Guidelines. Note that the sustainability policy does not specifically cover child labour, human trafficking or forced/compulsory labour.

- People Guide and HR processes: Based on Norwegian law and aligned with UNGPs/OECD; provides guidance to prevent and handle discrimination/harassment; mandates active, systematic equality work; HR risk assessments with employee representatives; corrective measures where risks are found; biannual gender pay gap mapping.

- Reporting channels: Multiple whistleblowing avenues (electronic, management, safety representatives, HR) to safely raise concerns about human and labour rights.

- Intended outcomes: Better working environment, higher engagement and productivity, and strengthened capability to deliver the Group’s sustainability and transition ambitions.

- ESRS references cited: ESRS 2 SBM‑3; ESRS S1‑1 and S1‑4; cross‑reference to ESRS E1‑3 (Climate change) for competence building.
text:
Governing documents
ESRS S1-1 Policies related to own workforce (incl. 
ESRS 2 MDR-P)
DNB’s Code of Conduct, Group policy for sustainability 
and People Guide (the Employee Handbook) determine 
how the Group should work with diversity and equality. The 
Code of Conduct is one of DNB’s governance principles 
documents and reflects DNB’s ambition to be a driving 
force for equality, diversity and inclusion. According 
134
DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Social conditions  > ESRS S1 Own workforceto the document, everyone in DNB is to be valued for 
their different qualities and allowed to be themselves. 
The Code of Conduct contains a prohibition against 
discrimination and harassment, and DNB does not accept 
any form of discrimination, whether this is on the basis 
of factors such as gender, age, ethnicity, religion, beliefs, 
disability, sexual orientation or political convictions. 
ESRS 2 MDR-P 
The Code of Conduct applies to all of the Group’s operations, 
including the international operations, and covers all activities 
and parts of the value chain. It applies to all permanent and 
temporary employees and includes consultants, as well as 
Board members and employee representatives. As is the case 
with the other governance principles, the Code of Conduct is 
approved by the Board of DNB Bank ASA. 
The operative responsibility for implementing and ensuring 
compliance with external and internal requirements, 
including the Code of Conduct, has been delegated to the 
Group Executive Vice Presidents and Managing Directors 
of the individual companies in the Group. Managers in DNB 
must ensure that employees understand the obligations 
set out in the Group’s governing documents, and that they 
take an active approach to compliance and complete the 
necessary training activities in their area of responsibility. 
As part of the operational risk management, each business 
area and Group unit must carry out ongoing internal 
control of compliance with the working environment 
legislation and rules relating to health, safety and the 
environment. This includes annual confirmation by each 
unit that the employees have read and understood the 
Code of Conduct. In addition, the implementation of 
the ambitions for diversity and equality in the Code of 
Conduct is indirectly monitored through the Group’s 
employee surveys, and discrimination is one of the areas 
the employees are asked about.
Internal stakeholders are involved in the work of preparing 
and updating the Code of Conduct. When making updates 
to governing documents that entail significant changes, 
the documents must be sent to mandatory consultation 
participants, including Group Audit, the control functions 
in the second line of defence, trade unions and the Group 
coordinator for corporate governance. Other relevant 
environments must also be considered for inclusion in the 
process. The Code of Conduct is available to employees 
through DNB’s internal quality system, in addition to being 
published on dnb.no .
According to the Group policy for sustainability, DNB 
must support and respect internationally recognised 
human rights and rights at work, including those laid down in the UN’s Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 
the UN’s International Covenant on Economic, Social 
and Cultural Rights, the UN’s International Covenant 
on Civil and Political Rights and the core conventions 
of the International Labour Organization (ILO). DNB 
must also perform a risk-based review of its own value 
chain in order to reveal the risk of actual and potential 
infringements of human rights and rights at work that DNB 
may cause, contribute to or be directly associated with 
in its capacity as employer. Based on the review, DNB will 
implement appropriate measures to stop, prevent or limit 
negative consequences in accordance with current rules 
and legislation and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational 
Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct (OECD 
Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises). 
The minimum disclosure requirements (ESRS 2 MDR-P) 
relating to information about the Group policy for 
sustainability are described on page 112 under Governing 
documents in the sub-chapter ESRS E1 Climate change. 
The policy does not specifically cover child labour, human 
trafficking, forced labour or other compulsory labour.
DNB’s People Guide is based on Norwegian legislation, 
which is also in line with internationally acknowledged 
standards, such as the UN Guiding Principles on 
Business and Human Rights and the OECD Guidelines 
for Multinational Enterprises. The guidelines mainly 
contain information and guidance for managers and 
employees, while regulating the prevention and handling 
of discrimination and harassment, and they are designed 
to promote an equal and diverse working environment. 
The Group’s policies and rules are operationalised through 
various procedures to ensure that differential treatment 
is prevented, reduced and followed up. According to the 
statutory provisions, DNB must work actively, purposefully 
and systematically to promote equality and prevent 
discrimination at the workplace. Risk assessments are 
carried out for various HR processes, with the participation 
of the employees’ representatives, and measures are 
implemented if risk of discrimination or obstacles to 
equality are detected. In addition, the pay gap between 
women and men is mapped every two years. Other 
examples of how the Group works to promote diversity 
and equality are described under Actions (ESRS S1-4). 
The Group has established several channels that 
employees can use to report unacceptable circumstances. 
Whistleblowers can use an electronic channel or contact 
the management, the safety representative function or 
the HR unit. This creates a safe platform for addressing 
concerns relating to human rights and rights at work.

title: Interaction with own employees
heading: 5.1.1.3 Interaction with own employees
start_phrase: The Group has several processes where the management has a dialogue with the employees, including through trade unions.
summary:
- Scope: ESRS S1-2 (engagement with own workforce and worker representatives) and ESRS S1-3 (remediation processes and channels to raise concerns).
- Social dialogue and collective bargaining: DNB engages regularly with several trade unions; six unions represent over half of employees. Dialogue occurs via quarterly Group- and unit-level meetings and additional information/consultation meetings at multiple organizational levels. Decisions affecting employees are made within these forums, aligned with legislation, collective agreements, and internal practice. Responsibility sits with the Head of Governance and Strategy in HR, within the employer policy governance function.
- Effectiveness: No direct measurement system; low levels of conflict are used as a proxy for effective, balanced cooperation. Employee representatives are involved before decisions are made.
- Employee feedback and workplace climate: Annual working environment survey maps experiences of discrimination and unfair treatment, informing D&I strategy, goals, and measures, elevating the topic for discussion and providing guidance on actions and support. Managers are trained to detect and address discrimination and support vulnerable employees.
- D&I governance and networks: Dedicated D&I officers in every business area and Group unit ensure leadership support and integration of D&I in product and service development. Active employee-run networks (with HR support) cover equality, multicultural diversity, LGBT+, and an internal ODA network for women in technology, providing additional employee insights.
- Complaint and whistleblowing channels: Employees can report concerns via management, HR, safety representatives, or an external whistleblowing channel (varsling@dnb.no), with further details referenced under ESRS G1. Complaints are handled confidentially, respecting legal and agreed confidentiality. DNB promotes psychological safety to lower the threshold for speaking up.
- Case handling and remediation: Depending on case nature, HR engages appropriate resources (coaches, HR, legal, HSE), while internal audit or legal handle whistleblowing cases. Annual surveys map unfair treatment to guide preventive work and scope, with measures implemented as needed.
- Awareness and accessibility: Notification channels are communicated through internal webpages and information materials, with ongoing mapping to ensure visibility and use.
text:
Interaction with own employees
ESRS S1-2 Processes for engaging with own workforce and 
workers’ representatives about impacts
The Group has several processes where the management 
has a dialogue with the employees, including through 
trade unions. There are several trade unions in DNB, and 
at present, the Group’s social dialogue in Norway is based 
on collective agreements that have been entered into 
with six trade unions that represent more than half of the 
employees. There is cooperation between the management 
and the employee representatives on a regular basis, which 
helps ensure proper working conditions in DNB. At the 
same time, the dialogue between employer and employee 
representative on work-related questions helps strengthen 
the employer’s decision-making basis. The cooperation 
with trade unions at Group level and in the business areas 
and Group units takes place at regular quarterly meetings. 
In addition, information and consultation meetings are 
regularly carried out with the employee representatives 
at the organisational levels mentioned, as well as at lower 
levels. Decisions are made at these meetings that affect 
the employee’s interests This takes place in accordance 
with provisions in legislation and collective agreements, 
as well as DNB’s administrative practice. Responsibility for 
the social dialogue with the trade unions at Group level 
lies with the head of governance and strategy in the HR 
unit. This unit is part of a broader function with governing 
responsibility for DNB’s employer policy.
DNB does not have any processes that directly measure the 
effectiveness of the cooperation, but the fact that there are 
few conflicts relating to the social dialogue is a sign that it 
is effective and balances employer and employee interests 
appropriately. The cooperation takes place under agreed, 
predictable terms, with employee representatives being 
brought in before decisions are made. 
Employees are invited to give feedback through employee 
surveys. Experiences of discrimination and unfair treatment 
are mapped in the annual working environment survey. 
The results provide input to the strategy for diversity and 
inclusion work, and to goals and measures. Another desired 
effect of examining this topic is that it is regularly escalated 
for discussion in the organisation. At the same time, it 
gives an opportunity to provide information about what 
action to take in connection with such incidents and where 
employees can get help if they need it. Great emphasis is 
placed on enabling managers to detect discrimination and 
1 The ODA network: Voluntary organisation by and for women in the Norwegian technology sector.unfair treatment, and to providing care and good follow-up 
to employees who are in a vulnerable situation.
DNB has also established dedicated diversity and inclusion 
officers in every business area and Group unit, and these 
are responsible for securing support from management, 
driving the agenda in their unit and ensuring that diversity 
and inclusion are safeguarded in product and service 
development. The Group has established active networks for 
equality, multicultural diversity, gender and sexual diversity 
(LGBT+), as well as an internal ODA network 1 for women 
in technology. These networks are run by employees, with 
support from the HR unit. DNB also gains insight into the 
employees’ perspectives through these networks.

title: Notification channels
heading: 5.1.1.4 Notification channels
start_phrase: If an employee feels that they are being subjected to differential treatment or discrimination, or they experience other negative incidents, they can report this through different channels.
summary:
- Focus area: ESRS S1 (Own workforce) covering engagement with employees and representatives, grievance/whistleblowing channels, and actions on material workforce impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Social dialogue and collective bargaining: DNB maintains structured engagement with multiple trade unions (six in Norway, representing over half of employees) under collective agreements. Regular quarterly meetings occur at Group, business area, and unit levels, with additional information/consultation forums where decisions affecting employees are made in line with laws and agreements. Responsibility sits with HR’s head of governance and strategy within a central employer policy function.
- Effectiveness of engagement: No direct measurement framework, but low levels of conflict indicate effective, balanced cooperation. Employee representatives are consulted before decisions.
- Employee feedback and inclusion: Annual working environment surveys map experiences of discrimination and unfair treatment, informing D&I strategy, goals, and measures, and ensuring regular organisational discussion and guidance on reporting and support. Managers are trained to detect and address discrimination and support vulnerable employees.
- D&I governance and networks: Dedicated D&I officers in every business area/unit drive the agenda and embed D&I in products/services. Active employee-run networks (with HR support) include equality, multicultural diversity, LGBT+, and an internal ODA network for women in technology, providing insight into employee perspectives.
- Grievance and whistleblowing: Multiple confidential channels for reporting discrimination/unfair treatment (management, HR, safety reps, external whistleblowing channel). Emphasis on psychological safety and low reporting threshold. Cases are handled by appropriate functions (HR, legal, HSE, internal audit) and, when needed, external specialists; corrective measures may occur at individual and system levels.
- Awareness and training: Information on channels via intranet, materials, and surveys; mandatory annual Code of Conduct training covers how and why to report concerns. DNB monitors and follows up issues raised and collaborates with stakeholders to ensure channel effectiveness.
- Actions on material impacts and risks (2024): Updated D&I strategy (originally 2022) with new measures to increase women in management after a decline in levels 1–4; gender balance embedded in strategic job transitions. Requirements include: identifying top male and female finalists in management recruitment; targets of at least 50% women in leadership/talent programs and 40% women on successor lists; emphasis on gender balance when changing management team composition.
- Risk assessment and mitigation: Systematic 2024 risk assessments per Anti-Discrimination Act across recruitment, pay/conditions, promotions, development, facilitation, work–family balance, and risks of harassment/sexual harassment/gender-based violence; integrated into operational risk management. No new risks requiring additional measures beyond ongoing operations. Mitigation centers on Code of Conduct adherence, bias awareness, competence building, and regular training for managers and safety reps with clear escalation duties.
- Roles and accountability: Central HR ensures compliance with anti-discrimination protections and leads D&I measures; a dedicated subject-matter expert supports these topics; HR manages Group-level employer responsibilities.
- Additional 2024 initiatives: Strengthened the multicultural diversity network to build awareness and competence (e.g., celebrating diverse festivals/holidays).
text:
Notification channels
ESRS S1-3 Processes to remediate negative impacts and 
channels for own workforce to raise concerns
If an employee feels that they are being subjected to 
differential treatment or discrimination, or they experience 
other negative incidents, they can report this through 
different channels. These include the management, the 
HR unit, direct contact with the safety representative by 
email or personal contact, as well as the Group’s external 
notification channel ( varsling@dnb.no ). See a more 
detailed discussion of the notification (whistleblowing) 
channel on page 157 under the topic Corporate culture 
(ESRS G1-1) in the sub-chapter ESRS G1 Business conduct.
DNB has established procedures for complaints 
processing associated with personnel matters. Complaints 
are handled confidentially and in accordance with the 
statutory and agreed duty of confidentiality. DNB works 
continuously on psychological safety to ensure that the 
threshold for raising concerns is low. Depending on the 
scope and nature of the matter, either HR is involved, 
using suitable resources like coaches, HR representatives, 
legal professionals or HSE officers, or the internal audit 
function or lawyers in connection with matters that are 
reported via the notification channel. Incidences of unfair 
treatment are mapped annually in connection with the 
working environment survey in order to create awareness 
and a discussion relating to preventive work with the issue, 
as well as to gain an overview of the scope of the situation. 
Measures are implemented as needed. 
DNB ensures that employees know about notification 
channels through information on internal webpages, 
in information material and through mapping using

they can report matters. There is also a digital training 
course on the Code of Conduct, which must be taken 
every year, that gives employees information about 
reporting unacceptable circumstances and encourages 
them to do so.
DNB monitors and follows up questions that are raised

title: Actions
heading: 5.1.1.5 Actions
start_phrase: Several measures have been implemented in the Group in connection with DNB’s work with diversity and equality and how it can affect employees positively by supporting equal opportunities.
summary:
- Reporting and conduct: Annual Code of Conduct training informs and encourages reporting of unacceptable circumstances; employee surveys check awareness of reporting channels. DNB monitors notifications, collaborates with stakeholders, and uses external specialists for complex discrimination cases; breaches may lead to individual and system-level corrective measures.

- ESRS S1-4 (Actions): Updated 2024 diversity and inclusion strategy (originally 2022) with new measures to lift women’s representation in management after a decline. Actions include:
  - Recruitment: identify the best qualified male and female candidates before final selection.
  - Talent/succession: target at least 50% female participation in leadership and talent programs and 40% women on successor lists; emphasize gender balance when reshaping management teams.
  - Risk management: systematic assessments of HR processes (recruitment, pay/conditions, promotions/development, facilitation, work–family balance) and risks of harassment/violence; 2024 assessments identified no additional required measures beyond ongoing work.
  - Mitigation: strengthen Code of Conduct compliance, address unconscious bias, regular manager and safety-rep training and escalation routines; central HR oversight with a dedicated expert.
  - Additional measures: strengthened multicultural diversity network (awareness, celebrations, role models), celebrations of International Women’s and Men’s Days, and two disability-focused digital courses with Stiftelsen VI.

- Measuring effectiveness: Ongoing evaluations of courses/events; employee surveys, risk assessments, and notification insights. Inclusion score target ≥5/6; Q4 2024 result 5.3 with 80% response rate. Results are externally processed and reported to Group Management and the Board. Legal limits on demographic data constrain identification of underrepresented groups. Premises follow local universal design/building regulations.

- ESRS S1-5 (Targets/metrics): No time-bound diversity/equality targets, but an ongoing 40/60 gender balance ambition at all management levels (1–4). Tracked quarterly across the Group (excluding managers on leave and a specified subsidiary), reported to the Board; metrics not externally validated beyond the auditor.
  - 2024 outcomes: Women at management levels 1–4 averaged 36.5% (down from 38.8% in 2023); Board 50.0% women; Group Management 41.7%.
  - Breakdown: Levels 1–2: 42.9% women (6/14); Level 3: 39.4% (41/104); Level 4: 35.6% (153/430).

- ESRS S1-6 (Workforce characteristics): As of 31 Dec 2024, total employees 11,515: 6,183 men, 5,332 women; “Other” and “Not reported” both 0. Figures may differ from financial note disclosures due to inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., employees on leave, AAP, certain subsidiaries).
text:
actions
Several measures have been implemented in the Group 
in connection with DNB’s work with diversity and equality 
and how it can affect employees positively by supporting 
equal opportunities. These are Group-wide activities, with 
a few constraints relating to DNB’s international offices, 
out of consideration for local law and practices.
In 2024, DNB updated the Group’s strategy for diversity 
and inclusion that was launched in 2022. The strategy 
describes the diversity areas that have been prioritised, 
and their levels of ambition. In 2024, new measures to 
increase the proportion of women at management level 
were included, among other things. The reason for this 
is that the proportion of women at management levels 
1–4 fell somewhat in 2024. In order to follow this up 
further, gender balance was also included in strategic 
job transition management. In addition, DNB is working 
continuously to secure gender balance and sufficient 
access to female management talents by means of 
several measures, including the following: 
 →In recruitment processes for management positions, 
the best qualified male and female candidates, 
respectively, must be identified before a final 
choice is made. 
 →Gender balance must be taken into consideration 
in talent development, management development 
and successor planning. The target is a minimum of 50 per cent female participation in internal 
leadership development programmes and talent 
programmes, and 40 per cent women candidates on 
lists for successor planning. 
 →When changes are made to the composition of 
management teams, there must be a particular 
emphasis on achieving a better gender balance.
In 2024, DNB continued performing systematic risk 
assessments of central HR processes, in accordance with 
the statutory requirements in the Anti-Discrimination Act. 
The processes relating to recruitment, wages and working 
conditions, promotions and development opportunities, 
facilitation and opportunities for combining work and 
family life have been assessed. In addition, the Group 
looked at the risks associated with harassment, sexual 
harassment and gender-based violence. Risks relating 
to own employees are also an integral part of the 
operational risk management. 
In 2024, no risk was detected through the formal risk 
assessments that resulted in necessary measures 
or activities, other than the ongoing risk work and 
measures that are implemented in the ordinary 
operations. The main measures for mitigating risk are 
about ensuring compliance with the Code of Conduct 
in line management by increasing understanding of 
own attitudes and unconscious bias, as well as working 
with competence building. One of the most important 
measures that is carried out in DNB is therefore to 
regularly put the topic on the agenda. Managers and 
safety representatives receive training regularly and are 
made aware of the current guidelines against harassment 
and discrimination, as well as which notification channels 
are in force. Managers and safety representatives are 
responsible for escalating these matters in their areas. 
DNB’s central HR function ensures that the Group 
complies with the protection against discrimination and 
works on measures relating to diversity and equality. 
In addition, the Group has a dedicated subject matter 
expert who focuses on working with these topics. The HR 
unit also manages the Group’s employer responsibilities 
at a centralised level. 
Other measures relating to the work with diversity 
and equality in 2024: 
 →Strengthened the network for multicultural diversity 
that was established in 2022. The network works 
to increase awareness and competence relating to 
multicultural diversity by, for example, celebrating 
various festivals and holidays. The network also

DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Social conditions  > ESRS S1 Own workforceworks actively to showcase role models with a 
multicultural background through interviews and 
posts on internal webpages. 
 →Celebrated International Women’s Day and 
International Men’s Day. 
 →Launched two digital courses on disabilities for 
DNB employees in collaboration with the equal 
opportunities foundation Stiftelsen VI.
DNB measures and assesses the effectiveness of the 
various measures through ongoing evaluations of courses 
and events. In addition, employee surveys, risk assessments 
and notification via DNB’s established notification channels 
provide further insight to the work. DNB measures and 
follows up inclusion in DNB, among other things, based 
on answers to questions regarding perceived inclusion 
in the Group’s employee survey. The goal is a score of 
at least 5 on a scale of 1 to 6, and in the fourth quarter 
of 2024, the result was 5.3 among the 80 per cent of 
permanent employees who answered the survey. The 
metric is calculated by an external supplier who receives 
and processes employee data from DNB, and the 
result is reported to the Group Management team and 
the Board (ESRS 2 MDR-M). The working environment 
survey shows developments over time as the results are 
measured against the previous survey period. A large 
negative change may indicate a need for measures and 
will be followed up. There are statutory rules limiting 
the right to register and systematise the demographics 
of the workforce, which makes it difficult to identify 
underrepresented groups and implement targeted efforts 
to control developments quantitatively. 
The work with diversity and equality is a continuous 
process of improvement and covers all grounds for 
discrimination and minorities. In order to avoid a 
significant negative impact on DNB’s own workforce, 
work is done to increase compliance with guidelines and 
regulations through the measures mentioned. In relation 
to universal design of premises, DNB follows the building 
regulations in every country in which the Group operates.

title: Targets and tracking
heading: 5.1.1.6.1 Targets and tracking
start_phrase: DNB does not have any time-specific targets for the topics diversity and quality but has an express ambition of a 40/60 gender balance at every management level (1–4) at any given time.
summary:
- DNB’s DEI initiatives include showcasing multicultural role models, celebrating International Women’s and Men’s Days, and launching two disability-focused digital courses for employees with Stiftelsen VI. The Group follows building regulations in all countries for universal design.
- Effectiveness is monitored via ongoing course/event evaluations, employee surveys, risk assessments, and whistleblowing channels. Inclusion is tracked through an employee survey (target ≥5/6); Q4 2024 result was 5.3 with an 80% response rate. An external supplier processes survey data; results are reported to Group Management and the Board. Trend analysis flags negative changes for follow-up.
- Legal constraints limit collection/systematization of workforce demographic data, complicating identification of underrepresented groups and targeted quantitative tracking.
- Targets and governance (ESRS 2 MDR-M; ESRS S1-5): No time-bound targets for diversity/equality, but an ongoing ambition of 40/60 gender balance at management levels 1–4 across the Group. Metrics are measured quarterly, followed up by each unit, and reported to the Board. Metrics have not been validated by any external party other than the external auditor.
- 2024 outcomes: Average women in management levels 1–4 was 36.5% (down from 38.8% in 2023). Board of Directors: 50.0% women; Group Management: 41.7% women. Management breakdown: Levels 1–2: 42.9% women (6) / 57.1% men (8); Level 3: 39.4% women (41) / 60.6% men (63); Level 4: 35.6% women (153) / 64.4% men (277).
- Workforce characteristics (ESRS S1-6) as of 31 Dec 2024: Total employees 11,515; men 6,183; women 5,332; “Other” 0; “Not reported” 0. Figures come from the internal HR system and differ from annual accounts due to exclusion of AAP recipients, employees on leave, and DNB Næringseiendom.
text:
Targets and tracking

title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 5.2.1.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: In DNB, consumers and end-users are referred to as customers.
summary:
- Scope and standards: ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users with links to ESRS 2 SBM-3 and ESRS S4-1, focused on data protection as a material topic for DNB’s customers (consumers and end-users).
- Material impacts, risks and opportunities: Handling large volumes of personal data for ~2.4 million customers; improper processing can cause legal breaches, fines, reputational loss, customer attrition and remediation costs; digitalisation and AI heighten data protection risks, making short‑term focus and long‑term risk management essential.
- Strategy and values: “Do the right thing” underpins compliance with data protection rules; maintaining customer trust is central; data protection integrated into technology solutions.
- Governance framework: Group-wide governing model for data protection with processes for secure storage, access control, internal controls, and monitoring legal changes; high priority on preventing breaches and safeguarding rights.
- Policies and documents (ESRS S4‑1): 
  - Code of Conduct (Board-approved) mandates lawful, transparent processing and immediate reporting of breaches.
  - Group Policy for Compliance (incl. GDPR adherence across jurisdictions).
  - Group Instructions for Personal Data Protection and a Global Framework for Personal Data Protection applying to all DNB entities.
  - Framework for the Data Protection Officer (DPO) function where appointed.
- Roles and responsibilities: Group EVPs accountable for compliance; all employees responsible for following rules; DPO monitors processing based on compliance and data subject risk; Compliance and Group Audit provide independent oversight.
- Training and awareness: Governing documents available in Norwegian/English; regular internal communication; mandatory e-learning on data protection with 92% employee completion in 2024; additional competence-building programs.
- Transparency and stakeholder communication: Privacy notices on dnb.no in relevant languages; customers informed via product terms; channels to ask questions or lodge complaints; ability to contact the DPO directly.
- Risk assessments and controls: Use of Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) for high-risk processing, with structured documentation ensuring accountability and verifiability; ongoing monitoring and control within each business area.
- Third-party expectations: Requirements for suppliers and partners via data processor agreements and third-party Code of Conduct.
- Human rights alignment: Commitment to internationally recognized human rights (UN declarations, covenants, ILO core conventions) and reference to OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises.
text:
In DNB, consumers and end-users are referred to as 
customers. DNB processes large amounts of personal 
data about its approximately 2.4 million personal 
customers. It is important that DNB processes the 
personal data of its customers in a secure way that instils 
trust and safeguards the customer’s right to protection 
of their personal data. If personal data is not processed 
properly, this may constitute a violation of the data 
protection rules and legislation and result in large fines 
and reputational loss. DNB has therefore identified that 
this can have a potential negative impact on and pose 
a risk to the customers. This is, not least, material in 
the short term, making it a matter that DNB must focus 
on. With increased digitalisation and use of artificial 
intelligence (AI), it is important that DNB continues 
to work in a targeted and long-term manner with data 
protection risk.
The value ‘Do the right thing’ is at the heart of the Group’s 
updated strategy, which also entails compliance with the 
data protection rules and legislation. It is important that 
DNB maintains a high level of trust among its customers, 
and the requirements relating to data protection are set 
out in the Group’s governing documents. DNB’s governing 
model for data protection is intended to contribute to 
the business areas complying with the data protection 
rules and legislation in their daily operations. The Group 
has internal processes and procedures for storing and 
managing personal data to prevent personal data from 
going astray and ensuring that it is managed satisfactorily. 
Secure and confidential management of personal data 
and protection of customers against breaches of the data protection rules and legislation is an important and 
prioritised area in DNB.
Ensuring compliance with the data protection rules and 
legislation is work that is done on an ongoing basis, 
and in DNB this is done, among other things, by training 
employees in the data protection rules and legislation, 
through internal controls and guidelines, by managing 
access control and by monitoring changes to the 
rules and legislation. Increased digitalisation makes it 
important that data protection is integrated well into 
the technological solutions. On dnb.no , customers can 
find information about how the DNB companies process 
personal data, what rights customers have, how they can 
contact DNB if they have questions about data protection 
and what options they have for making a complaint. 
Feedback from customers can help improve DNB’s work 
with data protection. If DNB does not ensure a good level 
of compliance with the rules and legislation, this can have 
a negative effect on DNB in the form of loss of customers 
and income due to a poor reputation, in addition to 
increased costs as a result of statutory fines. There will 
also be costs associated with remedying any issues 
resulting from non-compliance. 
Managing impacts, risks and 
opportunities

title: Governing documents
heading: 5.2.1.2 Governing documents
start_phrase: In DNB, all processing of personal data must be secure, transparent and understandable.
summary:
- Emphasis on building trust in DNB’s processing of personal data, with a duty for employees to report breaches of legal or internal rules; the Code of Conduct is Board-approved and public.
- Governance framework for data protection and compliance, including:
  - Group policy for compliance (GDPR and local laws).
  - Group instructions for personal data protection and a Global Framework for Personal Data Protection.
  - Framework for Data Protection Officer (DPO) function where required or adopted.
- Scope and applicability: covers all processing of personal data for customers, employees, and others across all DNB companies, including international operations, aligned with local laws.
- Clear roles and responsibilities:
  - Group EVPs accountable for compliance in their units.
  - All employees responsible for adhering to rules.
  - DPO monitors processing based on compliance and data subject risk.
  - Group Compliance and Group Audit provide independent oversight.
- Accessibility and training:
  - Governing documents available in Norwegian and English in the quality system.
  - Ongoing internal communications, guidelines on the intranet, and mandatory e-learning; 92% completion in 2024.
  - Additional courses and competence-building programs.
- Customer and partner transparency:
  - Privacy notice available online in multiple languages and embedded in product terms and agreements.
  - Expectations for suppliers and partners set via data processor agreements and a third-party code of conduct.
- Human rights alignment: commitments under UN human rights instruments and ILO core conventions.
- Risk management:
  - Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) for high-risk processing, with structured, quality-assured, and auditable documentation.
  - Obligation to report certain incidents to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority; 115 personal data breaches reported in 2024.
  - DPO monitors incidents and follow-ups with the Authority’s decisions.
- Complaints and whistleblowing mechanisms (ESRS S4-3):
  - Multiple channels: public notification email (varsling@dnb.no), online bank, customer service, direct DPO contact, and the right to complain to the Data Protection Authority.
  - DPO oversees complaint handling to protect rights and minimize negative impacts; multidisciplinary teams handle cases.
  - Strict confidentiality and access controls; options for anonymous contact.
  - External, independent management of the notification channel by NAVEX/GCS (EthicsPoint) ensuring confidentiality and no tracking.
  - Requirement that business partners provide anonymous, confidential whistleblowing channels.
  - While no explicit confidence assessments are made, incoming enquiries indicate awareness; visibility of channels is ensured and verified (including DPO info spot checks).
- Actions (ESRS S4-4):
  - Group-level measures and continuous, systematic efforts to minimize risks of personal data loss and maintain customer trust.
text:
suppliers, partners, employees and owners should have 
trust in DNB’s processing of personal data. If an employee 
becomes aware that personal data is being processed in 
breach of legal requirements or internal rules, they must 
notify their manager immediately. The Code of Conduct 
has been approved by the Board and is available to 
everyone on dnb.no . 
DNB has several other governing documents relating to 
compliance with current rules and legislation: 
 →Group policy for compliance: Its aim is to help DNB 
comply with rules and legislation, including the 
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), in each 
jurisdiction in which the Group has operations.
 →Group instructions for personal data protection: 
Their aim is to help DNB comply with the data 
protection rules and legislation, and they set out 
basic requirements for how the Group should process 
personal data. The instructions are elaborated on in 
DNB’s Global Framework for Personal Data Protection, 
which applies to all legal entities in the DNB Group. 
The framework is intended to help all companies in 
the Group process personal data in a responsible, 
lawful and secure manner. For the DNB companies 
that are required to appoint a Data Protection Officer 
(DPO) in accordance with the requirement in the 
GDPR, and for all DNB companies that voluntarily 
choose to appoint a DPO, the framework for the DPO 
function applies. 
The governing documents mentioned above cover all 
processing of personal data, which means all information 
about identifiable natural persons, including all customers 
and own employees. The governing documents apply to 
all companies in DNB, including the Group’s international 
operations, as long as this is consistent with local rules 
and legislation for companies in other countries than 
Norway. The Group Executive Vice Presidents (Group 
EVPs) of the various units in the Group have executive 
responsibility for ensuring compliance with the data 
protection rules and legislation. All employees are 
responsible for complying with internal and external 
rules and legislation. The DPO monitors the company’s 
processing of personal data based on compliance risk 
relating to the data protection rules and legislation, as 
well as the risk that the processing poses to the rights and 
freedoms of the data subjects.
The governing documents relating to data protection are 
available to all employees in DNB’s quality system, both 
in Norwegian and English, and they have been approved 
by the Group EVP of Group Compliance. Employees also have access to guidelines on the intranet, and information 
about data protection is regularly communicated via 
internal communication channels. Information about the 
main data protection obligations is also communicated 
through mandatory e-learning courses for the employees. 
In 2024, 92 per cent of the employees completed 
these courses. See Targets and tracking (ESRS S4-5) 
for a more detailed description of this metric. DNB also 
has programmes for courses and competence-building 
measures beyond the basic training. See Actions (ESRS 
S4-4) for a more detailed discussion of this. 
DNB’s privacy notice is available to customers and other 
stakeholders via DNB’s webpages. The privacy notice is 
available in Norwegian and English, and when relevant, 
also in local languages. In addition, relevant information 
is provided through agreements and the terms and 
conditions for various products and services. Customers 
can read about how DNB handles data protection on 
dnb.no . The Group informs suppliers and business 
partners about its expectations and requirements relating 
to the protection of people’s privacy rights through data 
processor agreements and DNB’s code of conduct for 
third parties. 
According to the Group policy for sustainability, 
DNB must respect internationally recognised human 
rights, including those laid down in the UN’s Universal 
Declaration of Human Rights, the UN’s International 
Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the 
UN’s International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights 
and the ILO core conventions. In order to reduce the 
risk of violations of data protection rules and legislation, 
DNB conducts a data protection impact assessment 
(DPIA) when it is deemed to be probable that a type 
of processing of personal data will entail a high risk to 
the rights and freedoms of natural persons. The work 
with DPIAs is organised in such a way as to safeguard 
quality, and the documentation is produced in a manner 
that creates accountability and verifiability. In addition, 
customers can contact the DPO if they believe that 
there has been a breach of the data protection rules and 
legislation. Each business area and Group unit in DNB is 
responsible for monitoring and controlling compliance 
with the data protection rules and legislation. From their 
independent position, the Group’s Compliance function 
and the DPO have special responsibility for monitoring 
and controlling compliance. In addition, Group Audit 
helps the Board ensure compliance with rules and 
legislation. 
It follows from the OECD Guidelines for Multinational 
Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct that

reasonable measures to ensure protection of the data 
they collect, store, use or disclose. DNB’s governing 
documents take the above-mentioned requirements into

title: Complaints processing
heading: 5.2.1.3 Complaints processing
start_phrase: Customers can report breaches of the data protection rules and legislation through DNB’s public notification channel ( varsling@dnb.no ) or contact DNB about privacy rights or other data protection-related questions and complaints through the online bank or via the customer service centre.
summary:
- Emphasis on customer privacy and data protection compliance: DNB’s governance incorporates legal requirements, and the bank must report certain incidents to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority.
- Incident oversight: 115 personal data breaches were reported in 2024; the Data Protection Officer (DPO) monitors incidents and DNB’s follow-up on Authority decisions.
- Complaints and reporting channels (ESRS S4-3): Customers can report data protection breaches via a public notification channel (varsling@dnb.no), through online banking, customer service, or directly to the DPO by email/post; unsatisfied customers can complain to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority. Information is available on DNB’s data protection webpages.
- Complaint handling approach: The DPO oversees complaint processing to protect customer rights and minimize negative impacts; cases are handled through dialogue and cross-functional collaboration (privacy experts, product specialists, lawyers, managers).
- Confidentiality and access control: Customer data is protected by statutory and contractual confidentiality; access is limited to need-to-know. Anonymous contact with the DPO is possible, and the DPO has a statutory duty of confidentiality. Anonymous reporting via the notification channel is supported, with strict confidentiality and limited case access.
- External whistleblowing system: DNB uses NAVEX/GCS Compliance Services Europe and the EthicsPoint platform for the notification channel, ensuring independence, EU hosting, and enhanced privacy (no IP tracking, phone number storage, or call recording). Further details referenced under Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1).
- Expectations for partners: Business partners must have anonymous, confidential whistleblowing processes that protect whistleblowers.
- Awareness and effectiveness: While no formal assessment of customer confidence is conducted, incoming enquiries indicate familiarity with complaint mechanisms. DNB ensures visibility of channels across webpages, materials, agreements, and product terms; verification occurs via product/service approval and DPO spot checks for DPO contact info.
- Actions and effectiveness (ESRS S4-4): Group-level measures are in place to reduce risks of data mishandling, address customer inconveniences, and sustain trust, with ongoing, systematic improvement efforts.
- Context: Content forms part of the Sustainability Report, Social conditions, ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users.

service centre. 
Customers can also contact the DPO directly by email or 
post. If a customer is not satisfied with how their enquiry 
is being handled, they can make a direct complaint to 
the Norwegian Data Protection Authority. Information 
about these options is available on DNB’s data protection 
webpages. 
The DPO monitors the processing of complaints and helps 
ensure that the rights and data protection of customers 
and end-users are protected, and that negative impacts 
on DNB’s customers are minimised. Complaints are 
handled by entering into a dialogue with the customer 
and collaborating internally to find a solution. If necessary, 
several employees in various roles will be involved in the 
management of a complaint and the response sent to 
the customer. This is often a combination of employees 
with competence on data protection, employees with 
expertise on the bank’s products and services, lawyers 
and managers, who familiarise themselves adequately 
with the customer’s situation and give reassuring feedback.
DNB’s management of customer data is subject to both 
a statutory and contractual duty of confidentiality, and 
only employees with a work-related need have access. 
This also applies to complaints processing. Employees, 
customers and other parties for whom DNB processes 
personal data can also contact the DPO anonymously. 
The DPO is subject to a statutory duty of confidentiality in 
their work. It is also possible to report matters anonymously using 
DNB’s notification channel. In such cases, personal data 
will not be registered. Notifications to varsling@dnb.no 
are treated confidentially, and the information provided 
in a notification, as well as information that comes to light 
during the processing, is only available to the people who 
process the case.
DNB uses the external company NAVEX/GCS Compliance 
Services Europe Unlimited Company, an independent 
service provider in the EU, and its software EthicsPoint to 
manage varsling@dnb.no . This secures full confidentiality 
for anyone who submits a notification. EthicsPoint is on 
NAVEX’ secure servers and is not part of DNB’s network 
or services. EthicsPoint does not track IP addresses or 
other data from the unit, nor does the program store 
phone numbers or record conversations. Read more 
about the notification channel on page 157 under the 
topic Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1) in the sub-chapter 
ESRS G1 Business conduct.
DNB requires that its business partners have notification 
processes that are known to the employees, and 
that these are anonymous, confidential and protect 
whistleblowers.
No explicit assessments are made as to whether 
customers and end-users have confidence in the 
notification and complaints processes relating to data 
protection, but the fact that DNB receives enquiries 
from customers indicates that they are familiar with 
the complaints mechanisms. In order to ensure that 
contact channels are available and known to customers, 
information about the channels is provided on DNB’s 
webpages, as well as in information material, in 
agreements and in product terms and conditions. This 
is verified through processes for approval of products 
and services, and by the DPO conducting spot checks of 
whether information about the DPO can be found in such 
information material.

title: Actions
heading: 5.2.1.4 Actions
start_phrase: To minimise the risk of personal data going astray and to be able to handle inconveniences to customers, DNB has implemented several measures at Group level.
summary:
- Commitment and obligations: DNB commits to respecting customer privacy and safeguarding personal data; it must report certain incidents to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (NDPA). In 2024, DNB reported 115 personal data breaches. The Data Protection Officer (DPO) oversees incident handling and follow-up on NDPA decisions.
- Complaints and reporting channels (ESRS S4-3): Customers can raise data protection concerns via DNB’s public notification channel (varsling@dnb.no), online bank, customer service, or directly to the DPO by email/post; if unsatisfied, they can complain to the NDPA. Information is available on DNB’s privacy webpages.
- Confidentiality and access control: Customer data handling (including complaints) is subject to statutory and contractual confidentiality; only employees with a work-related need have access. The DPO has a statutory duty of confidentiality and can be contacted anonymously.
- Anonymous whistleblowing: Anonymous reports are possible via the notification channel; personal data is not registered. Cases are handled confidentially and restricted to case processors.
- Independent whistleblowing system: DNB uses NAVEX/GCS Compliance Services (EthicsPoint) in the EU to manage varsling@dnb.no, ensuring full confidentiality; the system is separate from DNB’s network and does not track IPs or store phone numbers/recordings. Business partners are required to maintain anonymous, confidential whistleblowing processes.
- Awareness and verification: While no explicit confidence assessment is conducted, incoming enquiries suggest customers know the channels. Availability of contact information is ensured via webpages, materials, agreements, and product terms, with verification through product/service approval processes and DPO spot checks.
- Actions to strengthen data protection (ESRS S4-4):
  - Transparency and information: Ongoing improvements to privacy notices (bank, subsidiaries, EU branches) begun in 2023 and continuing in 2025 to make information clearer and current.
  - Competence and culture: Annual data protection month, lectures with internal/external experts, interactive exercises, and a new internal data protection podcast launched in 2024, with more planned in 2025.
  - Accountability and internal guidelines: New operational privacy framework consolidating guidance and clarifying roles/responsibilities; new AI guidelines highlighting privacy considerations; applicable Group-wide.
  - Effectiveness and incident management: Compliance controls and internal audits assess effectiveness; incidents handled via Group instructions and a common non-compliance system with documented actions; DPO advises on protecting affected parties; customers are informed of high-risk breaches and may seek compensation, complain to NDPA, or pursue court claims.
  - Governance integration: Data protection is embedded in corporate governance, aligned with the Group compliance policy, operational incident management, and supplier-related security/risk management frameworks; NDPA supervises Norwegian companies.
- Organization and resources: Approximately 45 employees work full-time or near full-time on data protection across business areas and Group units, including a central operational privacy team and dedicated legal resources. The DPO acts independently, advises, monitors compliance, and serves as the point of contact for NDPA and data subjects; local DPOs support international offices.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS S4-5):
  - Policy approach: No specific numeric target; compliance with laws is mandated via the Code of Conduct and compliance policy. Compliance risk is managed by Group-wide criteria; practices include regulatory monitoring, personal data procedures, and employee training; ongoing controls, audits, and risk reporting inform continuous improvements.
  - Tracked metrics (externally verified):
    - Fines from NDPA related to GDPR breaches: None received in 2024 (confirmed by the Group Secretariat).
    - Number of non-compliance reports to NDPA (personal data breaches): Identified via a predefined report from the non-compliance system (2024 figure reported earlier as 115).
    - Percentage of employees completing four mandatory data protection courses: Tracked via the Motimate learning platform as of 31 December 2024 (excludes external consultants).

actions
To minimise the risk of personal data going astray and 
to be able to handle inconveniences to customers, 
DNB has implemented several measures at Group 
level. DNB wants to maintain the customers’ trust and is 
therefore continuing the ongoing and systematic work
