title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 6.1.2.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: DNB has identified corruption and bribery as material risks that can affect the Group’s own operations.
summary:
- Focus area: Corruption and bribery as a material risk within DNB’s own operations, especially where employees interact with external parties.
- Strategic context (ESRS 2 SBM-3): Rated most material in the short term due to potential impacts on reputation, trust, fines, financial losses, share price, and cost/access to capital.
- Cultural foundation (ESRS G1-1): Emphasis on strong corporate culture and business ethics to maintain stakeholder trust; continuous efforts to uphold and improve ethical standards.
- Prevention and detection: Ongoing risk assessments, employee training, and internal controls to monitor and report suspicious activities.
- Anti-corruption framework: Group-wide ABC (anti-bribery and corruption) programme to meet national and international laws, with requirements for top-level commitment, risk assessments, documented routines/processes, customer and other due diligence, communication/training, and control/follow-up.
- Governance and accountability: Group EVP for Group Compliance holds ultimate responsibility; Group Compliance monitors adherence and maintains the framework, considering criminal, financial, and reputational risks.
- Policies and instructions: Zero tolerance for corruption embedded in the Code of Conduct, Group anti-corruption instructions, and a global anti-corruption framework; mandatory employee awareness via the internal quality system.
- Supporting policies: Code of Conduct complemented by conflict-of-interest management and whistleblowing instructions.
- Reporting and disclosures: References to minimum disclosure requirements (ESRS 2 MDR-P) and links to ESRS S1 Own workforce for Code of Conduct governance.
text:
DNB has identified corruption and bribery as material risks 
that can affect the Group’s own operations. The risks are 
concentrated in areas where there is interaction between 
DNB employees and external parties.
DNB places great emphasis on a corporate culture that 
promotes good business ethics in order to maintain trust 
among customers, stakeholders and society in general. 
Read more under the topic Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1) 
in the sub-chapter ESRS G1 Business conduct. 
Corruption and bribery cases can have serious 
consequences for reputation and trust, and may lead 
to fines and financial losses for the Group, in addition 
to a decline in the share price, increased cost of capital 
and reduced access to capital. The work to prevent and 
detect corruption and bribery takes place on a continuous 
basis, and in the materiality analysis it was assessed as 
being most material in the short term. 
Continuous work is done to ensure that ethical standards 
are maintained and improved, both to protect DNB’s 
financial stability and reputation and to handle the risk of 
losses for the Group, investors and other stakeholders. 
DNB has implemented measures to handle the risk of 
corruption and bribery in its own operations, including by 
having a Group-wide anti-corruption (ABC) programme 
to ensure that the Group complies with national and 
international corruption rules and legislation. Risk 
assessments are carried out regularly, as well as employee 
training, and internal control mechanisms have been 
established to monitor and report suspicious activities. 
These measures contribute to reducing the risk of 
corruption and protecting DNB’s reputation and financial 
stability. Managing impacts, risks and 
opportunities
Governing documents 
ESRS G1-1 Corporate culture and business conduct policies

title: Governing documents
heading: 6.1.2.2.1 Governing documents
start_phrase: According to the Code of Conduct, DNB has zero tolerance for all forms of corruption, and the Group must actively prevent and detect corruption by ensuring that all employees are familiar with and follow established rules and routines, as well as by reporting any suspicion of corruption.
summary:
- Focus: DNB’s approach to corruption and bribery under ESRS G1 Business conduct (ESRS 2 SBM-3, G1-1, G1-3, G1-4, MDR-A/MDR-P).
- Materiality and strategy: Corruption and bribery are identified as material, near‑term risks, especially where employees interact with external parties. Potential impacts include reputational damage, fines, financial losses, share price decline, and higher capital costs. DNB emphasizes a strong ethical culture and continuous prevention/detection to protect financial stability and trust.
- Governance and accountability: Zero‑tolerance set out in the Code of Conduct, Group anti‑corruption instructions, and a global anti‑corruption (ABC) framework requiring top‑level commitment, risk assessments, due diligence (customer and other), communication, training, controls, and follow‑up. The Group EVP for Group Compliance is responsible for implementation; Group Compliance (second line) monitors and reports to Management and the Board; Group Audit (third line) independently investigates and reports to the Board. Whistleblowing and conflicts‑of‑interest policies support the framework. All governing documents are accessible internally and managers must ensure staff understanding and training.
- Prevention and detection: Units must tailor procedures based on ABC risk assessments across their value chains. Suspicion is handled via incident management and whistleblowing channels. Training is risk‑based with three competence levels: mandatory annual digital courses for all employees, plus enhanced/dilemma training and topical seminars for higher‑risk roles. High‑risk functions include direct customer contact, procurement, contract awarding, and hiring. Training also covers the Board and Group Management. Course completion is tracked.
- 2024 actions: Updated governing documents; introduced a gifts and business entertainment register for transparency and documentation; adopted a more quantitative methodology for company‑specific risk assessments. All measures implemented and applicable to all employees.
- Metrics/outcomes: No convictions or fines for breaches of anti‑corruption or anti‑bribery legislation in 2024.
text:
Governing documents 
ESRS G1-1 Corporate culture and business conduct policies
According to the Code of Conduct, DNB has zero 
tolerance for all forms of corruption, and the Group must 
actively prevent and detect corruption by ensuring that 
all employees are familiar with and follow established 
rules and routines, as well as by reporting any suspicion of 
corruption. 
The Group instructions for anti-corruption set out zero 
tolerance for corruption, and are intended to ensure that the 
Group prevents, detects and manages corruption in all parts 
of the operations. The Group also has a global framework 
for anti-corruption. The governing documents require 
that DNB’s ABC programme has top-level commitment, 
risk assessments, routines and processes, customer due 
diligence, other due diligence, communication and training, 
as well as control and follow-up.
The Group Executive Vice President (Group EVP) for 
Group Compliance has ultimate responsibility for 
implementing the current instructions and framework 
in the Group. The Group unit Group Compliance is 
responsible for monitoring compliance relating to anti-
corruption. This includes preparation and maintenance of 
DNB’s anti-corruption framework. DNB plays an important 
role as a responsible player in Norwegian society, and 
the considerations of criminal liability, financial loss and 
reputational loss have been assessed when preparing the 
instructions and the framework for anti-corruption. 
The governing documents are available in the Group’s 
internal quality system, and it is a requirement that 
all employees are familiar with the content of the 
instructions.
The minimum disclosure requirements (ESRS 2 MDR-P) 
relating to the Code of Conduct are described on page 
134 under Governing documents (ESRS S1-1) in the sub-
chapter ESRS S1 Own workforce.
The Code of Conduct is elaborated on in the Group 
policy for managing conflicts of interest and the Group 
instructions for whistleblowing. See a more detailed

 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Governance information  > ESRS G1 Business conductdiscussion of the whistleblowing channel on page 157 
under the topic Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1) in the 
sub-chapter ESRS G1 Business conduct.
Managers must ensure that employees understand the 
obligations set out in the governing documents, that they 
take a proactive approach to compliance and that they 
complete the necessary training activities. Furthermore, 
the Group instructions for anti-corruption include training 
and set out detailed requirements that are adapted to the 
employees’ roles and responsibilities. 
Read more about the units in DNB that are most exposed 
to corruption and bribery under Prevention and detection 
of corruption and bribery (ESRS G1-3).

title: Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
heading: 6.1.2.2.2 Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
start_phrase: The Code of Conduct, the Group instructions for anti-bribery and the Group’s anti-corruption framework describe what corruption is and provide guidance for employees on how to prevent and detect it.
summary:
- Focus on DNB’s governance of anti-corruption and bribery under ESRS G1 (Business conduct), with references to whistleblowing channels detailed in Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1).
- Manager responsibilities: ensure employees understand governing documents, adopt a proactive compliance mindset, and complete role-adapted training.
- ESRS G1-3 framework: Code of Conduct, anti-bribery instructions, and a global anti-corruption framework define corruption and guide prevention/detection.
- Unit-level implementation: each unit must build procedures and processes based on ABC (anti-bribery and corruption) risk assessments across value chains; controls and training support the program.
- Reporting and investigation: suspicions are handled via incident management and whistleblowing; Group Audit (third line) investigates notifications and can use external resources; Compliance (second line) reports to Group Management and the Board; Group Audit is independent and reports to the Board.
- Training program: documents accessible to all; annual mandatory digital training for all employees; three risk/competence levels with risk-based depth; additional targeted training (e.g., dilemma training, seminars) for higher-risk roles; coverage includes customer-facing, procurement, contract awarding, hiring, as well as the Board and Group Management.
- 2024 actions: updated governing documents; introduced a gifts and business entertainment register for transparency; adopted a more quantitative, company-specific risk assessment methodology; measures implemented group-wide.
- Metrics/outcomes (G1-4): no convictions or fines for breaches of anti-corruption/anti-bribery laws in 2024.
text:
Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery 
The Code of Conduct, the Group instructions for anti-
bribery and the Group’s anti-corruption framework 
describe what corruption is and provide guidance for 
employees on how to prevent and detect it. Each unit in 
DNB must develop and integrate their own procedures 
and processes based on the ABC risk assessment in the 
unit’s value chains. In addition, training is provided and 
there are controls relating to the anti-corruption work. 
Suspicion of corruption is addressed in accordance with 
the procedures for managing incidents and through 
whistleblowing. 
As the third line of defence, Group Audit investigates and 
manages notifications relating to corruption and bribery. It 
is also possible to use external resources for incidents when 
necessary. Read more about the Group’s whistleblowing 
channels under the topic Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1) in 
the sub-chapter ESRS G1 Business conduct.
DNB’s compliance function is part of the Group’s 
second line of defence and reports to both the Group 
Management team and the Board. Group Audit is 
independent of the Group’s executive management 
and reports incidents to the Board of Directors of 
DNB Bank ASA. 
The Group instructions for anti-corruption are available 
to all employees through the Group’s quality system, 
and it is a requirement that everyone is familiar with this 
document. This is followed up annually through the metric 
for proportion of completed courses. Reference is also 
made to other relevant documents in digital courses. The anti-corruption training is based on responsibility, 
role and function. Three levels of competence have 
been defined that reflect this, and there are different 
requirements for each competence level. The scope and 
intensity of training is risk-based. Different competence 
levels with associated competence requirements 
and training measures follow from DNB’s global anti-
corruption framework. Annual basic digital courses that 
are mandatory for all employees cover DNB’s global anti-
corruption framework, identification and management of 
corruption risk, as well as the consequences of corruption. 
Relevant additional training for employees for whom the 
risk is assessed as being higher focuses on more detailed 
knowledge of the framework, dilemma training and 
topical seminars.
Functions that are exposed to risk are functions with high 
inherent corruption risk, for example areas with direct 
customer contact, and functions in purchasing, contract 
awarding and hiring. In departments that are exposed to 
risk, every function is covered by the training programme. 
This also includes training for the Group’s administrative, 
management and control bodies, which in DNB are the 
Board and the Group Management team. 
Actions 
ESRS 2 MDR-A

title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 6.1.3.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: Financial crime, which includes fraud, money laundering and sanctions violations, poses a serious societal problem and a threat to our welfare system, while also undermining a healthy business sector.
summary:
- Focus area: Financial crime (fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations) as a material topic for DNB, despite not being covered by topical ESRS standards.
- Context and impacts: Significant societal and financial sector risks; negative impacts include customer harm, fraud losses, investigation costs, fines, and compensation claims. Positive impact stems from DNB’s role in safeguarding a secure financial system benefiting customers, investors, and society.
- Risk horizon: Impacts and risks arise primarily from DNB’s own operations and secure digital systems; considered short term but critical for long-term viability due to persistent, evolving threats requiring continuous monitoring and security updates.
- Strategy and governance (ESRS 2 SBM-3; ESRS 2 MDR-P; ESRS G1):
  - Code of Conduct: Commitment to actively prevent and detect money laundering and terrorist financing.
  - Governing documents:
    - Handling of external fraud: Detect and prevent external data fraud; Group Security division sets processing rules and investigates cases.
    - Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT): Defines expected controls, roles, and oversight; Group AML Manager accountable for follow-up.
    - International sanctions: Group-wide sanctions compliance program to prevent violations and circumvention; outlines controls and roles.
- Implementation and oversight: Policies available to all employees via the internal quality system; business area and unit managers responsible for compliance and implementation under DNB’s governance model.
- Reporting: Periodic risk and compliance reporting provides the DNB Bank ASA Board with status and relevant updates.
text:
Financial crime, which includes fraud, money laundering 
and sanctions violations, poses a serious societal problem 
and a threat to our welfare system, while also undermining 
a healthy business sector. As Norway’s largest financial 
institution and an important party in the financial system, 
DNB plays a significant role in limiting financial losses 
for society, customers and other stakeholders. This topic 
is not covered by the topical ESRS standards but is 
nevertheless considered a material topic for DNB. 
Financial crime can have a negative impact on customers 
and poses a financial risk for DNB. Losses resulting 
from fraud, costs associated with investigations 
and prosecutions, and potential fines and claims for 
compensation may affect the Group's financial results. 
DNB can also have a positive impact in this area, as the 
Group has an important position in the financial system 
relating to ensuring a safe financial sector, which benefits 
customers, investors and society. Threats such as fraud, 
money laundering and sanctions violations are persistent 
challenges that require continuous monitoring and 
updating of security measures. 
The Group's positive and negative impacts, as well as the 
identified risks, are associated with DNB's own operations 
through the use of safe and secure digital systems. These 
are considered to have a short-term perspective, as 
DNB must focus on them now in order to be viable in the 
future.

title: Governing documents
heading: 6.1.3.2.1 Governing documents
start_phrase: According to the Code of Conduct, DNB will actively prevent and detect money laundering and terrorist financing by following established rules and internal procedures for anti-money laundering and combatting the financing of terrorism.
summary:
- Topic and materiality: Financial crime (fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations) is not a topical ESRS standard but is deemed a material topic for DNB due to its societal impact and DNB’s role as Norway’s largest financial institution.
- Impacts, risks, opportunities: Financial crime can harm customers and create financial risks for DNB (fraud losses, investigation costs, fines, compensation claims). DNB can also have a positive impact by safeguarding the financial system for customers, investors, and society. Threats are persistent, requiring continuous monitoring and security updates. Impacts and risks stem from DNB’s own operations and secure digital systems, with a short‑term focus critical to future viability.
- Governance and policies (ESRS 2 MDR-P): 
  - Code of Conduct commits to preventing and detecting money laundering and terrorist financing.
  - Handling of external fraud policy covers detection and prevention of external data fraud; Group Security leads investigations and rules.
  - AML/CFT governing document sets expected controls and roles; Group AML Manager oversees procedures.
  - International sanctions governing document defines the sanctions compliance program and control expectations.
  - Documents are accessible in the internal quality system, apply to all employees; business area/unit managers ensure implementation. Periodic risk and compliance reporting informs the Board. Cross-reference to Code of Conduct disclosures under ESRS S1-1.
- Actions and resources in 2024 (ESRS 2 MDR-A):
  - Updated Global AML Framework to ensure compliance, consistency across Norway and international operations, and guidance on laws and regulatory expectations; Group Compliance owns the document and conducts regulatory monitoring via RegChange in BWise.
  - Updated Group-wide inherent money laundering/terrorist financing risk assessment (DNB ML‑TF IRA) to guide local risk assessments, resource allocation, customer risk classification, and due diligence; enhances business-wide awareness and compliance with national/international requirements.
  - Updated Group-wide sanctions risk assessment to inform entity-level assessments, strengthen controls, identify new mitigating measures, and raise awareness of sanctions exposure, using insights from DNB operations, peers, and external sources.
  - Developed a new, standardized, more quantitative methodology for business-specific risk assessments across AML, anti-corruption, and sanctions to align with regulatory expectations and ensure clear linkage between risk assessments and controls.

Governing documents
ESRS 2 MDR-P Policies adopted to manage material 
sustainability matters
According to the Code of Conduct, DNB will actively 
prevent and detect money laundering and terrorist 
financing by following established rules and internal procedures for anti-money laundering and combatting 
the financing of terrorism. 
DNB also has several other governing documents that 
focus on combatting financial crime.
 →The governing document Handling of external fraud 
covers the efforts to detect and prevent fraud, 
including data fraud carried out by external players 
with or without a contractual relationship with 
DNB. The Group Security division is responsible for 
handling external fraud and prepares processing 
rules, as well as being the unit that investigates such 
matters. 
 →The Group’s governing document Anti-money 
laundering and anti-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) 
covers DNB's work to prevent and detect whether 
customers misuse DNB for money laundering or 
terrorist financing. The document contains an overall 
description of what types of controls are expected to 
be in place and the Group’s different roles relating to 
anti-money laundering and combatting the financing 
of terrorism. The Group AML Manager has a specific 
responsibility for following up on the procedures. 
 →The governing document International sanctions 
describes DNB's Group-wide sanctions compliance 
programme. The purpose of the document is to 
ensure that DNB has necessary and robust measures 
in place to prevent violations of the sanctions rules 
and legislation, and to protect DNB from being 
misused to circumvent these rules and legislation. 
The instructions contain an overall description of what 
types of controls are expected to be in place and the 
different roles the Group has in the area of sanctions.
The governing documents are made available in 
the Group's internal quality system and apply to all 
employees. According to DNB’s governance model, 
the managers of each business area and Group unit are 
responsible for compliance with and implementation 
of the governing documents. Risk management and 
compliance are reported on periodically, and the 
reporting provides the Board of Directors of DNB Bank 
ASA with necessary information on relevant matters and 
status of the situation.

title: Actions
heading: 6.1.3.3 Actions
start_phrase: Managing the negative impacts and risks that can arise from fraud and money laundering requires continuous monitoring and updating of security measures.
summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report (ESRS G1 Business conduct), noting where ESRS 2 MDR-P Code of Conduct disclosures are located, and focusing on ESRS 2 MDR-A (actions/resources) and ESRS 2 MDR-M (metrics) related to financial crime risk.
- 2024 actions to manage fraud, money laundering, terrorist financing, and sanctions risks:
  - Updated governing documents, including DNB’s Global AML Framework, to ensure consistent compliance across Norway and internationally; Group Compliance owns the framework and performs regulatory monitoring via RegChange in BWise.
  - Updated Group-wide inherent ML/TF risk assessment (DNB ML-TF IRA) to guide local risk assessments, resource allocation, customer risk classification, and due diligence across units and branches.
  - Updated Group-wide sanctions risk assessment to strengthen identification of required controls, harmonize practices, and reflect new insights from operations, peers, and external sources.
  - Developed a new, standardized, more quantitative methodology for business-specific risk assessments covering AML, anti-corruption, and sanctions, linking risk assessments to customer risk classification and transaction monitoring (Coverage Assessment). Risk is defined as threats exploiting DNB vulnerabilities; aims to improve efficiency, consistency, and compliance.
  - Measures apply to all employees, are ongoing and not time-limited; AML/CFT instructions are publicly available at dnb.no.
- Metrics and tracking of effectiveness:
  - Number of fraud cases handled in the alarm management system (calendar year).
  - Number of unique customers affected by fraud (annual).
  - Number of fraud incidents reported to the Norwegian police (annual; one report may cover many cases).
  - Total value of attempted fraud against customers and the Group that DNB stopped (annual).
  - Number of cases reported to Økokrim’s FIU (ongoing; all suspicious transactions are reported unless suspicion is disproven).
  - Number of frozen and reported transactions under sanctions rules and sanctioned-party lists (ongoing; all customers and transactions screened).
  - Percentage of employees completing annual AML/CTF training (mandatory).
- Collaboration: Continuous cooperation with the financial industry, Økokrim, and other authorities to protect customers and society from financial crime.
text:
Actions and resources in relation to material 
sustainability matters 
Managing the negative impacts and risks that can 
arise from fraud and money laundering requires 
continuous monitoring and updating of security 
measures. DNB works actively to combat financial 
crime, and in 2024, several measures were 
implemented to support this work.
 →DNB's governing documents relating to anti-money 
laundering and the combatting of terrorist financing 
were updated. DNB’s Global AML Framework is an 
internal framework for the efforts to prevent and 
detect money laundering and terrorist financing. 
The aim of the framework is to ensure that the 
Group complies with basic requirements and 
standards in this area, and to help ensure that the 
Group has a consistent approach, both in Norway 
and internationally. Furthermore, DNB’s Global AML 
Framework is intended to provide guidance for 
understanding applicable legislation, preparatory 
works and government guidelines. The framework 
is intended to provide support to Group functions 
and individual DNB entities, both when developing 
practical procedures/processes and when resolving 
specific issues. Group Compliance is the document 
owner and is responsible for regulatory monitoring 
in this area. The AML framework is thus a concrete 
expression of how Group Compliance believes 
the rules and legislation should be interpreted. 
Regulatory monitoring is carried out using 
RegChange in BWise, and new rules and legislation 
are implemented in the AML framework the next 
time it is updated.
 →DNB's Group-wide assessment of inherent money 
laundering and terrorist financing risk (DNB 
ML-TF IRA) was updated. The risk assessment is 
intended to provide business areas and Group 
units, international branch offices of DNB Bank ASA 
and companies in the DNB Group with an overall 
picture of which factors to take into account when 
preparing local risk assessments. The local risk 
assessments form the basis for, among other things, 
resource use in the entity and risk classification of the individual customer, which in turn form the basis 
for the implementation of customer due diligence 
and ongoing due diligence. The risk assessment 
helps DNB to continuously comply with national and 
international requirements to prepare a business-
specific risk assessment. The risk assessment is also 
intended to help increase awareness and knowledge 
of money laundering and terrorist financing risks 
in various parts of the DNB Group, and provide a 
basis for a more holistic approach to these risks, as 
well as to provide information on which units that 
prioritise preventing money laundering and terrorist 
financing.
 →DNB's Group-wide assessment of the risk of 
international sanctions violations was updated. 
The risk assessment provides an overall picture 
of which areas are to be included in the individual 
DNB entity's risk assessments, and which factors 
should be taken into account in each of the risk 
areas. The risk assessment also gives DNB a better 
basis for identifying the measures and controls 
required to handle sanctions risk, and to identify the 
need to implement new risk-mitigating measures 
and controls at Group level or at each DNB entity. 
Moreover, the risk assessment contributes to 
increasing awareness and knowledge within the 
Group of how DNB is exposed to sanctions risk and 
provides a basis for a more consistent and effective 
approach to the prevention of such risk. The risk 
assessment has taken into account new knowledge 
gained about exposure and development trends in 
relation to the risk of sanctions violations, based on 
experience and insight from DNB’s own business 
operations, other financial institutions and updated 
external sources that are relevant to DNB.
 →A new methodology for business-specific risk 
assessments was developed. Since the autumn of 
2023, Group Compliance has led a Group-wide 
project that has developed a new methodology for 
risk assessments, which will be used in the work 
relating to anti-money laundering, anti-corruption 
and sanctions. The background for this project was 
partly a desire to meet the expectations of the 
authorities and leading organisations for greater 
use of quantitative sources, and partly an intention 
to ensure a higher degree of standardisation and 
a more consistent approach to the methodology 
for preparing risk assessments across the Group. In 
addition, the project has aimed to ensure that there 
is a clear link between the risk assessments and the 
164
DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Governance information  > ESRS G1 Business conductrisk classification of customers, as well as between 
the risk assessments and the accuracy of scenarios 
in transaction monitoring (the Coverage Assessment 
tool). In short, in line with external practice, DNB 
has switched to a methodology where risk is 
defined as the ability of a threat to exploit DNB's 
vulnerabilities for the purpose of financial crime. 
DNB's exposure is factored in to a greater extent 
in the new methodology, and this – together with a 
more consistent and accurate methodology – will 
contribute to increased efficiency for DNB. The new 
methodology lays an important foundation for better 
risk management and compliance in the Group.
The measures that have been implemented to manage 
the negative impacts and risks that can arise as a result of 
fraud and money laundering apply to all employees, are 
worked on continuously and are not time-limited. 
The Group instructions for anti-money laundering 
and anti-terrorist financing are available to external 
stakeholders at dnb.no .

title: Metrics and targets - Introduction
heading: 6.1.3.4 Metrics and targets
start_phrase: To track the effectiveness of governing documents and goals and targets relating to financial crime, DNB monitors and reports on a selection of metrics on an ongoing basis, both internally and externally.
summary: DNB Group outlines ESRS 2 MDR-M and MDR-T metrics to track the effectiveness of its financial crime governance, working with the financial industry, Økokrim, and other authorities to protect customers and society against fraud. Defined metrics include: number of fraud cases handled in the alarm management system, unique customers affected, cases reported to the Norwegian police, total value of attempted fraud stopped, cases reported to Økokrim’s FIU (ongoing), number of frozen/reported transactions under sanctions rules (ongoing; all customers/transactions screened), and the percentage of employees completing mandatory AML/CFT training. Only statutory auditor assurance has been performed on these metrics. The 2024 results versus 2023 are: cases against customers 12,038 (9,723); customers affected 5,729 (5,010); police reports 47 (38); attempted fraud stopped NOK 2,137m (1,543m); FIU reports 3,478 (2,563); sanctions-related frozen/reported transactions 15 (4); AML/CFT training completion 92% (94%). DNB highlights continued investment in technology, monitoring and security system improvements, cooperation with public authorities, and internal training to combat financial crime.
text:
Metrics and targets 
Targets and tracking
ESRS 2 MDR-M Metrics in relation to material sustainability 
matters
To track the effectiveness of governing documents 
and goals and targets relating to financial crime, DNB 
monitors and reports on a selection of metrics on an 
ongoing basis, both internally and externally. The Group 
works closely with the financial industry, Økokrim (the 
Norwegian National Authority for Investigation and 
Prosecution of Economic and Environmental Crime) 
and other government bodies to protect customers and 
society in general against fraud. 
The method and assumptions applied to the various 
metrics are described below.
Number of cases against customers:  
This metric shows the number of cases associated with 
fraud targeting all DNB customers, which the Group has 
handled in its alarm management system from 1 January 
2024 to 31 December 2024. The metric has been used 
for a long time to show the number of cases relating to 
customers in the alarm management system for fraud. A 
customer can be linked to several cases.
Number of customers affected by fraud:  
This is the number of unique customers who were affected by fraud in the reporting year. The number differs from the 
previous metric as the same customer can be exposed to 
fraud several times. This can include both different types 
of fraud and the same type over a long period of time. 
Number of cases of fraud reported to the Norwegian 
police:  
This is the number of incidents reported to the police in 
the reporting year, based on an assessment of all cases 
handled by the alarm management system. The metric is 
used to show activity in the form of reported incidents. 
A report that is filed with the police may cover a number 
of large cases involving many customers, and cases are 
reported to the police following an overall assessment.
Total value of attempted fraud against customers and 
the Group that was stopped:  
The total potential losses associated with attempted 
fraud that were stopped by DNB’s actions during the 
reporting year. This shows the value of the attempted 
fraud stopped by DNB. 
Cases reported to Økokrim's FIU (the Norwegian 
National Authority for Investigation and Prosecution 
of Economic and Environmental Crime):  
This metric is not time-limited and cases are reported to 
Økokrim on an ongoing basis throughout the year. The 
metric is used to track the effectiveness and follow up 
on the goal of reporting all suspicious transactions to 
Økokrim.
Matters should be reported to Økokrim if suspicion of 
money laundering has not been disproven. Reporting 
suspicious transactions and matters to Økokrim helps 
ensure a stable financial sector and supports the active 
fight against financial crime.
Number of frozen and reported transactions in 
accordance with the sanctions rules and legislation 
and the list of sanctioned persons or companies:  
This metric shows the number of frozen and reported 
transactions under the sanctions rules and legislation and 
the list of sanctioned persons or companies. The metric 
is part of DNB's monitoring of sanctions. All customers 
and transactions are monitored and checked against the 
sanctions list, and these processes are not time-limited. 
Percentage of employees who completed annual 
training in anti-money laundering and combatting of 
terrorist financing:  
This metric shows the percentage of DNB employees who 
have completed the mandatory courses on anti-money 
laundering and the combatting of terrorist financing.

These courses are designed to ensure that all employees 
have knowledge about money laundering and terrorist 
financing, why this is important and the responsibility 
that lies with each employee. Training is an important 
part of DNB's commitment to combatting financial crime. 
By ensuring that employees complete the mandatory 
courses, DNB can strengthen its overall efforts to combat 
financial crime and reduce the risk associated with this.
The metrics mentioned above provide good insight into 
how effectively the Group handles cases relating to 
financial crime. Good monitoring systems and continuous 
improvement of security systems are measures that have 
been initiated to handle fraud using DNB's systems. DNB 
will continue its work on investing in new technology, 
cooperating with public authorities and providing internal 
training to support its ambition to combat financial crime. 
The only validation that has been carried out of these

title: Targets and tracking
heading: 6.1.3.4.1 Targets and tracking
start_phrase: No measurable and result-oriented targets have been set in relation to financial crime.
summary:
- Focus on DNB’s efforts to combat financial crime, emphasizing mandatory employee training in anti‑money laundering (AML) and counter‑terrorist financing (CTF), individual responsibility, and continuous improvement of monitoring and security systems.
- Commitment to investing in new technology, cooperating with public authorities, and strengthening internal capabilities to reduce fraud risk and support a secure digital economy.
- Metrics for 2024 (with 2023 comparisons) used to track effectiveness:
  - Cases against customers: 12,038 (9,723 in 2023)
  - Customers affected by fraud: 5,729 (5,010)
  - Fraud cases reported to Norwegian police: 47 (38)
  - Attempted fraud value stopped: NOK 2,137 million (NOK 1,543 million)
  - Cases reported to Økokrim’s FIU: 3,478 (2,563)
  - Sanctions-related frozen/reported transactions: 15 (4)
  - Employees completing annual AML/CTF training: 92% (94%)
- Only validation of these metrics is assurance by the statutory auditor.
- Under ESRS 2 MDR-T (tracking effectiveness), DNB states it has not set measurable, result-oriented targets for financial crime yet.

- Effectiveness is tracked via annual, Board‑approved Group-wide inherent risk assessments for ML/TF and sanctions violations, with ongoing risk identification and public transparency through published advice, threat assessments, and related reports.
text:
No measurable and result-oriented targets have been set 
in relation to   financial crime. To ensure that the work to 
combat financial crime is effective, DNB must:
 →know its customers, business partners and suppliers;
 →monitor transactions to and from accounts in DNB;
 →understand, manage and assess the risks to which the 
Group is exposed, and 
 →take a holistic approach to its work, across specialist 
areas and business areas.
To track the effectiveness of current policies and actions, 
DNB prepares Group-wide assessments of the inherent 
risk of money laundering and terrorist financing and 
international sanctions violations. Inherent risk is defined 
as the risk that exists before control measures are taken 
into account. The risk assessment is carried out annually 
and is approved by the Board. DNB also publishes advice 
and recommendations, an annual report on DNB’s threat 
assessment and other reports on DNB’s website, so that 
they are made available to everyone. The work to identify 
the inherent risk is done on an ongoing basis, and follow-
up of the work is described above, under Targets and 
tracking.

title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: 6.1.4.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: As a systemically important financial institution in Norway 1, DNB plays a critical role in maintaining financial stability in the Norwegian economy.
summary:
- Company-specific topic: Financial infrastructure and financial stability, framed under ESRS 2 SBM-3 and ESRS 2 MDR-P; not covered by topical ESRS but deemed material for DNB.
- Role and context: DNB is designated a systemically important financial institution in Norway, with a critical role in sustaining national financial stability and essential public services.
- Strategy: Focus on securing a stable and safe digital economy through robust action plans, risk management, and crisis management to ensure operational stability and resilience.
- Risks and impacts: System disruptions and downtime (e.g., payment services) pose financial risks (lost income, higher costs) and reputational risks (loss of customer trust), with societal implications; maintaining stability underpins trust in the broader financial system.
- Time horizon: Assessed as most relevant in the short term to ensure future viability.
- Governance and policies: Board-approved Group Principles for Risk Appetite serve as the overarching governance document for risk control, including operational risk and operational stability; aims for effective risk identification, handling, monitoring, and reporting, and alignment with the Group’s risk tolerance; accessible to employees via the internal quality system.
- Scope: Principles apply across all DNB operations globally and to business partners acting on DNB’s behalf.
- Responsibilities and oversight: Group Risk Management develops the principles; a second-line coordinator is assigned per risk dimension to monitor adherence, trigger follow-up, and implement action plans if limits are breached; structure supports the first line of defence.
text:
As a systemically important financial institution in 
Norway 1, DNB plays a critical role in maintaining financial 
stability in the Norwegian economy. Any disruptions 
to systems relating to the delivery of essential public 
services can have negative consequences for customers 
and society as a whole. 
DNB’s strategic focus is on securing a stable and safe 
digital economy, which is critical to both DNB’s own 
viability and the financial health of society. This is why 
it is important for DNB to have sound action plans and 
risk management systems in place to manage potential 
threats and possible crises. 
Disruptions to systems, such as downtime, constitute a 
financial risk to the Group’s profitability in addition to 
reputational risk, as this can damage customers’ trust 
in DNB. Downtime in payment services, for example, 
entails a risk of loss of income and increased costs. 
By maintaining stability, DNB can also help sustain 
trust in the financial system in society in general. By 
keeping a continuous focus on operational stability, risk 
management and crisis management, DNB contributes 
to ensuring financial stability in the economy. This is 
done, among other things, through action plans to ensure 
financial stability and to restore operations in the case of 
disruptions, as well as to set the limits for acceptable risk. 
The topic has been identified in the materiality analysis 
as most relevant in the short term, as this is something 
that DNB must focus on today to be viable in the future. 
It is not covered by the topical ESRS standards but is 
nevertheless considered a material topic for DNB.
1 The Ministry of Finance has decided that DNB is a systemically important financial institution in Norway, in accordance with the recommendation 
from Finanstilsynet (the Financial Supervisory Authority of Norway).Management of material impacts, risks 
and opportunities
Governing documents
ESRS 2 MDR-P Policies adopted to manage material 
sustainability matters

title: Governing documents
heading: 6.1.4.2.1 Governing documents
start_phrase: In order to maintain financial stability, it is important that DNB works to manage risk that can affect the financial infrastructure, and thus stability.
summary:
- Focus: DNB’s role in safeguarding financial infrastructure and stability as a systemically important financial institution in Norway; company-specific, short‑term material topic under ESRS 2 SBM‑3, not covered by topical ESRS but deemed material for DNB.

- Strategic intent: Ensure a stable, secure digital economy to protect DNB’s viability and broader financial health; continuous emphasis on operational stability, risk management, and crisis management to maintain trust and reduce disruptions (e.g., payment downtime) that carry financial and reputational risks.

- Governance and policies (ESRS 2 MDR‑P):
  - Group-wide Risk Appetite Principles approved by the Board, covering operational risk and stability; designed for effective risk identification, handling, monitoring, and reporting.
  - Applicability across all DNB operations and relevant partners; developed by Group Risk Management.
  - Second-line coordinators per risk dimension oversee adherence and trigger action plans if limits are breached; first line accountable for execution.
  - Regular reporting: quarterly to the Board; monthly to Group Management.
  - Internal stakeholder consultation on significant document updates; documents accessible via the internal quality system.

- Capabilities and criticality management:
  - Group instructions define a capability model and a Group-wide criticality scale (72-hour perspective) to prioritize and coordinate during crises.
  - Distinguishes critical, significant, and other capabilities; identifies those critical for society (financial stability) versus DNB-critical.
  - Governance: Group EVP Technology & Services owns the models; strategic ownership of critical capabilities at Group EVP level in business areas/units.
  - Annual assessments and business impact analyses required; policies apply to all employees and Group entities, including international operations.

- Business continuity and cyber security:
  - Group instructions for business continuity set requirements for managing serious disruptions; related cyber security details referenced under ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users.

- Actions and resources (ESRS 2 MDR‑A):
  - Preventive measures: regular risk assessments, robust internal controls, and continuous monitoring of external threats; ongoing effort to reduce vulnerabilities and sustain operations during crises.
  - Recovery plan and crisis management aligned with BRRD II, integrated into risk and capital management; covers DNB Bank ASA and subsidiaries across geographies.
  - Key components: risk assessments, crisis management plans, and communication plans.
  - Acknowledges local regulatory/cultural constraints; mapped and mitigated (e.g., increasing asset liquidity to enable efficient crisis disposals).

- Outcomes sought: Minimize incident probability, protect profitability and reputation, preserve customer trust, and contribute to overall financial system stability.
text:
Governing documents
ESRS 2 MDR-P Policies adopted to manage material 
sustainability matters
In order to maintain financial stability, it is important that 
DNB works to manage risk that can affect the financial 
infrastructure, and thus stability. The Group’s document 
containing the principles for risk appetite in DNB is 
the overarching document that sets out requirements 
relating to governance and control of risk in DNB, and 
describes risk appetite relating to, among other things, 
operational risk, including operational stability. The aim 
of the document is to contribute to ensuring effective 
identification, handling, monitoring and reporting of 
relevant risks in DNB. The document also contributes 
to plans and activities being carried out in accordance 
with the Group’s risk tolerance, and thus reducing the 
probability of unwanted incidents. The document is 
available to the employees through DNB’s internal quality 
system.
The principles for risk appetite have been approved 
by the Board of Directors of DNB Bank ASA and have 
been integrated into the Group’s risk management. 
The principles and the guidelines apply to all of the 
DNB Group’s operations, regardless of geographical 
location, customer groups and organisational affiliation. 
Business partners are also included when they act on 
behalf of DNB. The Group unit Group Risk Management is 
responsible for developing the principles for risk appetite. 
In order to ensure implementation of the principles, a 
coordinator has been established in the second line of 
defence for each risk dimension. The coordinator is also 
responsible for initiating follow-up and, if applicable, 
implementing relevant action plans if limits are broken. 
The purpose is to ensure that the first line of defence 
167
DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Governance information  > ESRS G1 Business conductestablishes any necessary actions, and that all managers 
in DNB are responsible for doing their work in accordance 
with set risk principles and risk tolerances. The status of 
the risk appetite is reported to the Board every quarter 
through the risk report. The Group Management team 
also receives a monthly report that shows the status in 
relation to the risk appetite limits. 
Internal stakeholders are involved in the work of preparing 
and updating the principles. When updates to governing 
documents entail significant changes, the documents 
must be sent to mandatory consultation participants, thus 
ensuring that the interests of internal stakeholders are 
safeguarded.
The Group instructions for capabilities and criticality 
are two significant governing documents because they 
contain information about what DNB must prioritise 
during crises to maintain stability, as well as which parts 
of DNB’s value chain are critical. A capability is DNB’s 
ability to perform a given task, such as payment services 
or operation and maintenance of the IT infrastructure 
that supports DNB’s services. Critical capabilities are 
necessary to maintain DNB’s ability to deliver services and 
products reliably, even under challenging conditions. 
The Group instructions for capabilities describe DNB’s 
Group-wide capability model, which shows the most 
important functions that DNB delivers. The model 
illustrates important value chains and distinctions 
between critical, significant and other capabilities. This 
makes it easier to set priorities during crises and ensure 
that the most important functions are operational. Critical 
capabilities can be critical for society (critical for financial 
stability), or they can be DNB-critical (critical or important 
for DNB). 
DNB’s Group instructions for criticality contain a 
Group-wide scale that can be used for prioritisation 
and coordination and ensures that all business areas 
and Group units have good governance and control 
of what is critical in a 72-hour perspective. The scale 
is used to identify critical capabilities and functions. 
These instructions are important to contribute to DNB 
maintaining stability and infrastructure also during crises. 
The Group Executive Vice President (Group EVP) 
of Technology & Services is responsible for the 
capability model and for the Group-wide model for 
the assessment of criticality. Strategic ownership of 
the critical capabilities is placed at Group EVP level 
in responsible business areas and Group units. At a 
minimum, the Group EVPs must ensure that the critical capabilities are assessed once a year. The Group EVPs 
are also responsible for business impact analyses being 
performed to assess criticality in own areas, so that 
DNB has an overview of what is critical. The instructions 
apply to all permanent and temporary employees of the 
Group, as well as all companies in the Group, including its 
international operations. The documents are available to 
all employees in the internal quality system.
DNB’s Group instructions for business continuity are also 
important, as they set out the requirements for preparing 
the Group to manage serious business and operational 
disruptions. Read more about the instructions under 
the topic Cyber security in the sub-chapter ESRS S4 
Consumers and end-users. 
Actions
ESRS 2 MDR-A

title: Actions - Introduction
heading: 6.1.4.2.2 Actions
start_phrase: In order to prevent the potential negative impact and the risk that may arise if DNB does not maintain stable operations and the financial infrastructure, and to ensure the customers’ trust in the financial system, DNB carries out a number of preventive measures.
summary: Overview of DNB Group’s preventive actions and resources to manage material sustainability risks tied to operational stability and financial infrastructure, emphasizing continuous risk assessments, robust internal controls, and external threat monitoring. Details a Group-wide recovery plan and crisis management framework aligned with BRRD II and integrated into risk and capital management, covering DNB Bank ASA and all subsidiaries across geographies with risk, crisis, and communication plans. Notes constraints from local regulations and cultural differences, mapped operational obstacles, measures such as increasing asset liquidity for efficient crisis disposals, and inclusion of critical sub-suppliers despite limited control over their full value chains. Describes plans to enhance emergency preparedness with regulators by updating procedures, ensuring legal/best-practice compliance, and expanding stress-testing to assess robustness, identify weaknesses, and define remediation. Mentions several Group-wide resilience measures implemented in 2024.
text:
Actions and resources in relation to material 
sustainability matters
In order to prevent the potential negative impact and 
the risk that may arise if DNB does not maintain stable 
operations and the financial infrastructure, and to ensure 
the customers’ trust in the financial system, DNB carries 
out a number of preventive measures. These include 
regular risk assessments, establishment of robust 
internal controls and continuous monitoring of external 
threats. Preventive measures have been developed 
to reduce vulnerabilities and improve DNB’s ability to 
maintain operations during a crisis. This work is done 
on a continuous basis. In addition, DNB’s recovery plan 
and crisis management work are important to secure 
resilience and the ability to manage crises, so that the 
bank’s stability is not affected. The recovery plan has 
been prepared in accordance with the Bank Recovery and 
Resolution Directive (BRRD II) and is an integral part of the 
Group’s risk and capital management framework 
The Group’s recovery plan and crisis management 
work are comprehensive and cover DNB Bank ASA and 
all of its subsidiaries. They apply across geographical 
areas and include a number of key elements such 
as risk assessments, crisis management plans and 
communication plans. However, the recovery plan has 
some delimitations due to local regulatory requirements 
and cultural differences. This can result in variations in 
how efficiently measures can be implemented in the 
countries in which DNB operates, but these operational 
obstacles have been mapped, and measures have been 
implemented to remedy this. One of the measures can 
be to increase the liquidity of DNB’s assets, which means 
that the disposal process in a crisis will be as efficient 
as possible. It is also important in this work to include 
168
DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Governance information  > ESRS G1 Business conduct
critical sub-suppliers in the risk assessments and the crisis 
management plans. However, there can be factors that 
limit the Group’s control and monitoring of these sub-
suppliers’ full value chain.
It is DNB’s aim to strengthen its emergency preparedness 
to maintain stability and its infrastructure though 
development of the recovery plan and the crisis 
management work. In the time ahead, DNB will focus 
on improving its internal crisis management framework 
in collaboration with the regulatory authorities. This 
includes evaluation and updating of procedures and 
guidelines to ensure compliance with best practices and 
applicable laws. A key part of this work is to expand the 
programme for stress testing of DNB’s ability to manage 
crises. Stress tests evaluate the Group’s robustness and 
emergency preparedness and identify weaknesses and 
areas for improvement, as well as necessary measures 
for crisis management. DNB’s continuous improvement 
of its crisis management capacity strengthens trust 
and secures financial stability and the Group’s ability to 
survive. In order to strengthen DNB’s resilience and ability 
to manage crises, DNB implemented several Group-wide 
measures in 2024. These are described below.

title: Changed the governance structure for the recovery plan
heading: 6.1.4.2.2.1 Changed the governance structure for the recovery plan
start_phrase: In 2024, DNB improved the efficiency of its crisis management by merging the central crisis management team and the recovery team into a single unit.
summary:
- Focus on strengthening DNB’s emergency preparedness and crisis management, including expanded stress testing to evaluate robustness, identify weaknesses, and define improvement measures.
- Inclusion of critical sub-suppliers in risk assessments and crisis plans, while noting limits to DNB’s control over sub-suppliers’ full value chains.
- 2024 governance change: merger of the central crisis management team and the recovery team to streamline decision-making and ensure consistency across the Group.
- Enhanced resolution planning: major internal crisis exercise, evaluation of the crisis framework, and new emergency preparedness plans for Financial Market Infrastructures to safeguard critical services and financial stability.
- Quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to assess overall recovery capacity, feasibility, synergies, and constraints.
- Stakeholder considerations: regulatory oversight for financial stability, customer expectations for protection of deposits/investments, and potential taxpayer exposure in severe crises.
- Metrics and monitoring per ESRS 2 (MDR-T/MDR-M): no single overriding CSRD target due to the risk-management nature and regulatory requirements; continuous processes to maintain stability via ongoing risk appetite monitoring across risk types, including operational and IT risk.
- IT stability tracking: monitoring days with moderate/significant customer-impacting incidents, color-coded (green/yellow/red); “red” days indicate significant operational incidents based on user experience.
text:
Changed the governance structure for the 
recovery plan
In 2024, DNB improved the efficiency of its crisis 
management by merging the central crisis management 
team and the recovery team into a single unit. This has led 
to the decision-making process for risk management and 
recovery planning being more efficient and consistent 
across the Group.

title: Updated the description of DNB’s efforts within resolution planning
heading: 6.1.4.2.2.2 Updated the description of DNB’s efforts within resolution planning
start_phrase: DNB continued to develop its crisis management capabilities in 2024, with a focus on operational preparedness and emergency preparedness planning.
summary:
- Focus on strengthening DNB’s emergency preparedness and financial stability through enhanced recovery planning, crisis management, and closer collaboration with regulators.
- Recognition of limited control over critical sub-suppliers’ broader value chains, while including them in risk assessments and crisis plans.
- Expansion of stress testing to assess robustness, identify weaknesses, and guide improvement measures in crisis management.
- 2024 governance change: merger of the central crisis management team and the recovery team to streamline decision-making and ensure consistency across the Group.
- Enhancements to resolution planning, including a major internal crisis exercise, framework evaluation, and new emergency preparedness plans for Financial Market Infrastructures to ensure continuity of critical services.
- Introduction of a quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to evaluate overall recovery capacity, feasibility, and potential synergies.
- Stakeholder considerations: regulatory oversight for financial stability, customer protection of deposits/investments, and potential taxpayer exposure in severe crises.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS 2 MDR-T): no single CSRD “overriding target” due to the risk-management nature and regulatory framework; instead, continuous processes to maintain stability.
- Ongoing monitoring of risk appetite and limit breaches across risk types, with particular emphasis on operational and IT risk.
- IT stability objective: minimize critical incidents; track days with moderate/significant customer-impacting IT events and classify them green/yellow/red, with “red” indicating a significant operational incident based on user experience.
text:
DNB continued to develop its crisis management 
capabilities in 2024, with a focus on operational 
preparedness and emergency preparedness 
planning. The Group conducted a significant internal 
crisis management exercise and evaluated its crisis 
management framework. DNB also developed 
emergency preparedness plans for its Financial Markets 
Infrastructures (FMIs), which are essential to maintain 
financial stability and ensure the continuity of critical 
services.

title: Quantified the effect of connections and dependencies on DNB’s total recovery capacity
heading: 6.1.4.2.2.3 Quantified the effect of connections and dependencies on DNB’s total recovery capacity
start_phrase: One of the main measures in the 2024 recovery plan was inclusion of a general quantitative analysis of connections and dependencies between different recovery alternatives and how these affect DNB’s overall recovery capacity.
summary:
- Focus on strengthening DNB’s crisis management and recovery capabilities to maintain financial stability and infrastructure, including integration of critical sub-suppliers in risk and crisis planning despite limited control over their broader value chains.
- Commitment to enhance emergency preparedness through collaboration with regulators, updating procedures and guidelines to align with laws and best practices, and expanding stress testing to assess robustness, identify weaknesses, and define improvement measures.
- 2024 organizational changes include merging the central crisis management team with the recovery team to streamline and harmonize decision-making across the Group.
- Ongoing development of resolution planning and operational preparedness, including a major internal crisis exercise and the establishment of emergency preparedness plans for Financial Market Infrastructures to secure continuity of critical services.
- Introduction of a quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to evaluate overall recovery capacity, feasibility, effectiveness, and potential synergies.
- Recognition of key stakeholders—regulators, customers, and taxpayers—and the importance of credible plans to protect deposits and maintain financial stability in crisis scenarios.
- Under ESRS-related disclosures, no single overarching CSRD target is set for financial stability due to its nature as a risk management domain subject to strict regulation; instead, stability is managed via established processes and risk appetite frameworks.
- Continuous monitoring of risk appetite across risk types, with a particular emphasis on operational and IT risk; tracking IT stability through the number of days with moderate or significant customer-impacting incidents, categorized green/yellow/red based on internal criteria, with “red” signifying significant operational incidents as experienced by users.
text:
One of the main measures in the 2024 recovery plan was 
inclusion of a general quantitative analysis of connections 
and dependencies between different recovery 
alternatives and how these affect DNB’s overall recovery capacity. The aim of the analysis was to provide a more 
objective and consistent assessment of the feasibility 
and effectiveness of the recovery plan, as well as to 
identify potential considerations and synergies among 
the recovery options. 
The work with recovery plans and crisis management 
affects several important stakeholder groups. The 
regulatory authorities play a key role in monitoring and 
regulating the activities of financial institutions to secure 
financial stability. DNB’s customers expect DNB to have 
sound plans to protect their deposits and investments 
in the event of a crisis, and Norwegian taxpayers can be 
affected if the Norwegian government has to intervene to 
save DNB in a crisis.

title: Targets and tracking
heading: 6.1.4.3.1 Targets and tracking
start_phrase: No overriding target in accordance with the disclosure requirements in the CSRD has been set to ensure that DNB maintains financial stability and its financial infrastructure because this is largely a matter of risk management.
summary:
- Focus on DNB’s crisis management and recovery planning: strengthening emergency preparedness, infrastructure stability, and collaboration with regulators; evaluating and updating procedures and guidelines; expanding stress testing to assess robustness and identify weaknesses and improvement areas.
- Limits to control over critical sub-suppliers’ full value chains acknowledged and incorporated into risk and crisis planning.
- 2024 Group-wide measures:
  - Merged central crisis management and recovery teams to streamline governance and decision-making.
  - Advanced resolution planning: ran a major internal crisis exercise, reviewed the crisis framework, and developed emergency plans for Financial Market Infrastructures to secure critical services.
  - Introduced quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to improve feasibility and effectiveness assessments and identify synergies.
- Stakeholder considerations: regulatory oversight for financial stability, customer protection expectations, and potential taxpayer exposure in crisis scenarios.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS 2 MDR-T):
  - No single overarching CSRD target due to the risk management nature and strict regulation; instead, continuous monitoring of risk appetite across risk types, including operational/IT risk.
  - IT stability tracked via “coloured days” (green/yellow/red) based on incident severity and customer impact; metrics verified by the statutory auditor.
  - 2024 outcomes: 4 red days (down from 7 in 2023) and 9 yellow days (down from 12).
  - Recovery plan includes early-warning metrics and predefined actions under a clear governance structure involving Group Management and the Board; plans reviewed annually by Norwegian and international regulators; sensitive details not disclosed per ESRS 1 §7.7.
- EU Taxonomy disclosures:
  - Mixed-group KPI overview shows average taxonomy-aligned ratios of approximately 4.8% (turnover-based) and 4.8% (Capex-based), with non-financial activities showing 0% alignment.
  - Asset manager KPIs: taxonomy-aligned investments represent about 2.3% (turnover-based) and 2.7% (capex-based) of assets covered; coverage ratio ~99%; most assets are not taxonomy-eligible; detailed breakdowns provided by geography, counterparty type, and environmental objective.
  - Environmental objective alignment primarily in climate change mitigation (including small shares of transitional and enabling activities); minimal to no alignment reported for other objectives (adaptation, pollution, biodiversity, water, circular economy except a small share).
text:
Targets and tracking
ESRS 2 MDR-T Tracking the effectiveness of policies and 
actions through targets (incl. ESRS 2 MDR-M)
No overriding target in accordance with the disclosure 
requirements in the CSRD has been set to ensure 
that DNB maintains financial stability and its financial 
infrastructure because this is largely a matter of risk 
management. In its role, DNB is subject to strong 
regulation in this area. This means that the Group must 
prevent disruptions from occurring and prepare action 
plans to restore its financial position or financial health 
if DNB’s operations are threatened. Several processes 
have been established to ensure that the stability is 
maintained. Among other things, DNB follows up its risk 
appetite relating to the various risk types on an ongoing 
basis, identifying the status of breaches of any limit 
values. Follow-up of the risk appetite ensures that the 
most material risks are followed up and managed in the 
operative parts of the organisation, including operational 
risk. When it comes to operational risk, IT stability is 
among the factors that are assessed, with a view to both 
future risks and past events, which gives a comprehensive 
overview of the Group’s IT risk. 
DNB wants to have stable IT operations that ensure 
satisfied customers, and to have a low number of critical 
IT incidents. The Group follows this up, among other 
things, by tracking the number of days with moderate 
or significant IT incidents that influence customers, 
and categorising the days green, yellow or red, based 
on internal assessment criteria. In order for a day to be 
categorised as red, a significant operational incident must 
have occurred. An operational incident is considered 
significant based on the users’ experience of problems 
169
DNB Group  Annual report 2024Contents
 > Management report  > Sustainability report  > Governance information  > ESRS G1 Business conductwith one or more of DNB’s IT systems, and may, for 
example, arise if the corporate online bank is down for a 
period of time. Yellow status means that there has been 
a moderate operational incident. For example, customers 
may have had problems logging in and their account 
data may be unavailable, and the incident is reported in 
the media. The criteria are quantitative and based on, 
among other things, how critical the IT system is when the 
downtime occurs, how long the downtime lasts and how 
large a proportion of the customers is affected. However, 
this differs from application to application in line with 
actual criticality. For example, the availability of online 
equity trading services will not be important when the 
stock markets are closed. 
The number of ‘coloured days’ is retrieved from an 
internal tool and is based on incidents in the past 24 
hours. This follows the incident management process 
described in DNB’s corporate governance documents. 
There is an annual risk assessment of the process, and in 
2023 an external audit of the process was carried out by 
DNB’s statutory auditor. The metrics are only verified by 
the statutory auditor.
2024 2023
Number of red days during the year 
(significant operational incident)4 7
Number of yellow days during the year 
(moderate operational incident)9 12
The number of days of operational incidents provides 
the basis for the risk appetite status that is reported to the Board and Group Management team every quarter. 
Measures are implemented to reduce the risk of new 
incidents based on the causes identified. The work is 
continuous and is not measured against a specific year. 
In 2025, the assessments of whether an incident causes 
a red, yellow or green day will be more closely linked to 
DNB’s critical capabilities.
The recovery plan also contains several metrics that 
indicate a possible deterioration in circumstances that 
may lead to activation of the recovery plan, and the plan 
gives clear guidelines as to which actions need to be 
implemented in a crisis. These measures must be carried 
out in accordance with an established governance 
structure that involves the Group Management team 
and the Board of DNB Bank ASA. Both Norwegian and 
international regulatory authorities have access to 
DNB’s recovery plan and crisis management work. These 
authorities approve and evaluate the plans every year to 
ensure that they meet all necessary requirements and 
standards. This annual evaluation helps maintain high 
quality in the crisis management process. For sensitivity 
reasons, the recovery plan and the crisis management 
work are not public information. The metrics have 
therefore not been reported, in accordance with ESRS 1 
paragraph 7.7 on classified and sensitive information.

- Asset managers’ KPI (Annex IV):
  - Weighted average taxonomy-aligned investments: NOK 16,928m (turnover-based) and NOK 20,293m (capex-based).
  - Assets covered by KPI (ex-sovereigns): NOK 740,580m; derivatives: NOK (1,756)m.
  - Exposure split vs Articles 19a/29a of Directive 2013/34/EU and EU/non-EU:
    - Subject to Articles 19a/29a: Non-financial NOK 143,400m; Financial NOK 90,304m.
    - EU not subject: Non-financial NOK 5,489m; Financial NOK 23,054m.
    - Non-EU not subject: Non-financial NOK 293,462m; Financial NOK 63,089m.
    - Other counterparties/assets: NOK 123,539m.
  - Taxonomy eligibility/alignment:
    - Not taxonomy-eligible: NOK 612,821m.
    - Eligible but not aligned: NOK 74,900m.
    - Taxonomy-aligned exposures (subject entities): Non-financial NOK 8,928m (turnover), NOK 13,776m (capex); Financial NOK 3,749m (turnover), NOK 2,753m (capex).
    - Aligned exposures to other counterparties/assets: NOK 4,251m (turnover), NOK 3,764m (capex).
  - Environmental objective breakdown (share of total assets covered, turnover/capex):
    - Climate change mitigation: 2.2% / 2.6% (of which transitional 0.2% / 0.3%, enabling 0.6% / 0.8%).
    - Adaptation, water/marine, pollution, biodiversity largely 0%; circular economy ~0.1%/0.1%.
  - Complementary disclosures:
    - Aligned exposures over assets covered: Non-financial (1.2% turnover; 1.9% capex), Financial (0.5% turnover; 0.4% capex), Other counterparties (0.6% turnover; 0.5% capex).
    - Eligible but not aligned over assets covered: 10.1%.
    - Weighted average aligned over assets covered: 2.3% (turnover), 2.7% (capex).
    - Coverage ratio (assets covered vs total AuM excl. sovereigns): 99.2%.
    - Denominator breakdown over assets covered: Derivatives (−0.2%); EU not subject: Non-fin 0.7% / Fin 3.1%; Non-EU not subject: Non-fin 39.6% / Fin 8.5%; Subject to Articles 19a/29a: Non-fin 19.4% / Fin 12.2%; Other counterparties/assets 16.7%; Not taxonomy-eligible 82.7%.
- Credit institutions’ KPIs (Annex VI):
  - Main KPI (GAR stock, 31 Dec 2024):
    - Environmentally sustainable assets: NOK 144,856m.
    - GAR: 5.18% (turnover-based) and 5.20% (capex-based).
    - Coverage over total assets: 88.59%.
    - Assets excluded from numerator: 39.10%; excluded from denominator: 11.41%.
  - Additional KPIs:
    - GAR flow: NOK 62,663m; 1.24% (turnover) and 1.36% (capex); coverage 73.42%; numerator exclusions 33.43%; denominator exclusions 26.58%.
    - Financial guarantees: NOK 188m; KPIs 2.42% and 1.90%. Trading book, AuM, and fees/commissions reported as i.a. (not applicable/available).
- Asset base for GAR calculation:
  - 2024 (turnover and capex views reported):
    - Total GAR assets: NOK 2,794,614m; assets not covered for GAR: NOK 360,111m; total assets: NOK 3,154,725m.
    - Covered assets include loans/advances, debt securities incl. use-of-proceeds, and equity not held for trading across financials, non-financials, and households.
    - Households (notably mortgages) form a large covered share (e.g., loans collateralised by residential property NOK 931,204m).
    - Items excluded from numerator but in denominator include SMEs/NFCs not subject to NFRD (NOK 708,913m), non-EU not subject (NOK 280,923m), derivatives (NOK 166,888m), interbank on-demand (NOK 4,764m), other assets (NOK 71,355m).
    - Off-balance sheet: financial guarantees NOK 7,766m with small aligned amounts.
  - 2023 comparatives provided with lower total assets and coverage, enabling year-on-year context.
- Sectoral (NACE) breakdowns of taxonomy-eligible and aligned exposures:
  - Presented for both turnover- and capex-based GAR, at 4-digit NACE, split between non-financial corporates subject to NFRD and SMEs/other NFCs not subject.
  - Key sustainable exposure areas include electricity production (NACE 3511), sea and coastal freight water transport (5020), service activities incidental to water transportation (5222), certain manufacturing (chemicals 2013/2014, steel 2410/2420, machinery 2892/2899), real estate activities (6820), and selective construction activities (4120, 4211).
  - Transitional and enabling shares are identified but remain modest across sectors.
- GAR KPI stock (turnover) 2024 – proportional view:
  - Aggregated shares of taxonomy-eligible vs aligned within the covered denominator; total aligned circa 5.18%, broadly consistent with the headline GAR.
  - Breakdowns by counterparty class (financials, non-financials, households) and by environmental objective show alignment concentrated in climate change mitigation, with negligible shares for adaptation, water/marine, circular economy, pollution, and biodiversity.

summary:
The excerpt presents DNB Group’s EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPI – stock (capex) for 2024. It details the GAR calculation with assets covered in both numerator and denominator, focusing on loans and advances, debt securities, and equity instruments not held for trading. The table breaks down exposures by counterparty type—financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations including investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, and households—and shows specific retail categories such as mortgages (loans collateralised by residential immovable property), building renovation loans, and motor vehicle loans. It distinguishes Use of Proceeds instruments and flags transitional and enabling activities.

For each category, the disclosure shows the proportions of total covered assets that are taxonomy‑eligible and taxonomy‑aligned, disaggregated across the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation, Climate Change Adaptation, Water and marine resources, Circular economy, Pollution prevention and control, and Biodiversity and ecosystems. A “Total GAR assets” line aggregates these metrics and notes an 88.59% figure relative to total covered assets in the denominator as of 31 December 2024. The content is part of the DNB Group Annual Report 2024 Sustainability Report section on the EU Taxonomy.

title: KPI off-balance sheet exposures flow (capex)
heading: 2.10 5. KPI off-balance sheet exposures flow (capex)
start_phrase: 1Financial guarantees (FinGuar KPI) 4,01 3,44 0,47 4,00 3,44
summary:
- Focuses on Section 5: EU Taxonomy KPIs for off-balance sheet exposures in DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report (Sustainability report, EU taxonomy section).
- Reports both stock and flow KPIs, each shown with turnover- and capex-based perspectives.
- Presents figures for two KPIs: Financial Guarantees (FinGuar KPI; with numerical percentages disclosed) and Assets under Management (AuM KPI; referenced but not populated in this excerpt).
- Breaks down results “of which” by Use of Proceeds, transitional activities, and enabling activities.
- Provides proportions of total eligible off-balance sheet assets that are taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned.
- Details the distribution across EU environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), including totals (e.g., CCM+CCA and full totals across objectives).
- Specifies the reporting date as 31 December 2024 for the proportions of covered assets funding taxonomy-relevant sectors.
